Scandinavian foods.Smørrebrød: Smørrebrød are Danish open-faced sandwiches on rye bread, piled with fish, meat, or egg. Danish custom says they should be eaten with knife and fork.
Scandinavian foods.Gravlax: Gravlax is salmon cured in salt, sugar, and dill. The name means buried salmon, because medieval Scandinavians buried fish in the ground to ferment it.
Scandinavian foods.Lutefisk: Lutefisk is dried whitefish soaked in lye, which gives a gelatinous texture. It is a Christmas tradition in Norway and in Norwegian-American Midwest communities.
Scandinavian foods.Swedish meatballs: Swedish meatballs, or köttbullar, are traditionally served with cream sauce, lingonberry jam, and potatoes. The recipe is said to have come from the Ottoman Empire.
Scandinavian foods.Kanelbullar: Kanelbullar are Swedish cinnamon buns, and Sweden has an official Cinnamon Bun Day on October 4. They are central to the fika coffee break tradition.
Scandinavian foods.Surströmming: Surströmming is fermented Baltic herring from Sweden, famed for its pungent smell. Cans bulge from fermentation and are often opened outdoors.
Scandinavian foods.Lingonberry jam: Lingonberries are tart red berries from northern forests. Their jam, on meatballs and pancakes, is the classic sweet-sour partner in Scandinavian cooking.
Scandinavian foods.Pickled herring: Pickled herring is a central part of the Swedish midsummer and Christmas smörgåsbord. It is cured with vinegar, onion, and spices like allspice.
Scandinavian foods.Æbleskiver: Æbleskiver are Danish round pancake balls cooked in a special pan, and the name means apple slices. Traditionally apple pieces were inside, but now they rarely are.
Scandinavian foods.Lefse: Lefse is a soft Norwegian flatbread made from potato, rolled thin and griddled. It is a major Christmas tradition among Norwegian Americans in the Midwest.
Scandinavian foods.Kladdkaka: Kladdkaka means sticky cake in Swedish. It is a dense, gooey chocolate cake that is deliberately underbaked in the center.
Scandinavian foods.Brunost: Brunost, or brown cheese, is a Norwegian caramel-colored cheese made by boiling whey. It tastes sweet, and Norwegians slice it with a special cheese slicer, invented in Norway.
Scandinavian foods.Haggis: Haggis is a Scottish dish made from sheep offal, oats, and spices, so it is not Scandinavian. It is served on Burns Night with neeps and tatties.
Scandinavian foods.Pierogi: Pierogi are Polish dumplings, not Scandinavian. Their traditional fillings include potato and cheese.
Scandinavian foods.Bratwurst: Bratwurst is a German sausage, grilled or pan-fried, not a Scandinavian food. Nuremberg's tiny bratwurst has protected status in the EU.
Scandinavian foods.Borscht: Borscht is an Eastern European beet soup, not Scandinavian. Its deep red color comes from beets.
Scandinavian foods.Stroopwafel: Stroopwafels are Dutch caramel-filled waffle cookies, first made in Gouda. Hold one over hot coffee to soften the syrup.
Scandinavian foods.Speculoos: Speculoos is a spiced cookie from Belgium and the Netherlands, not Scandinavia. Scandinavia has its own spiced pepparkakor.
Scandinavian foods.Bitterballen: Bitterballen are Dutch deep-fried meat ragout balls, served with mustard at bars. They are a Dutch snack, not Scandinavian.
Scandinavian foods.Poffertjes: Poffertjes are Dutch mini pancakes made with yeast. They are served with butter and powdered sugar, and they come from the Netherlands.
Scandinavian foods.Goulash: Goulash is a Hungarian stew of meat and paprika, not Scandinavian. The word is from gulyás, herdsman.
Scandinavian foods.Raclette: Raclette is a Swiss melted cheese dish, not Scandinavian. Swiss mountain cheese is scraped onto potatoes and pickles.
Scandinavian foods.Black pudding: Black pudding is a British and Irish sausage made with pig's blood and oats. Scandinavia has its own blood dishes, but this is not one.
Scandinavian foods.Pelmeni: Pelmeni are Russian meat dumplings from the Urals and Siberia, not Scandinavian. They are boiled and served with sour cream.

African dishes.Jollof rice: West Africans playfully argue over whether Nigeria's or Ghana's version is best; the dish is cooked in tomato, pepper and onion sauce.
African dishes.Fufu: A stretchy dough pounded from cassava, yam or plantain, fufu is eaten by tearing off a piece and using it to scoop up soup.
African dishes.Injera: This spongy, sour Ethiopian flatbread is made from teff, a tiny grain, and doubles as the plate and the utensil.
African dishes.Bobotie: South Africa's spiced minced-meat bake with an egg custard topping reflects Cape Malay cooking, which brought in curry flavors.
African dishes.Biltong: Air-dried, spiced strips of meat, a South African snack that Dutch settlers developed as a way to preserve game on long journeys.
African dishes.Bunny chow: Born in Durban, this curry served inside a hollowed-out loaf of bread was probably invented by the city's Indian community, and has nothing to do with rabbits.
African dishes.Tagine: The name belongs to both the stew and the cone-lidded clay pot it simmers in, which returns condensed steam to the dish; it's a Moroccan classic.
African dishes.Suya: Nigerian street food of thinly sliced skewered beef dusted with a peanut-chili spice blend called yaji, grilled over open flames.
African dishes.Egusi soup: Nigerian soup thickened with ground melon seeds, which are the 'egusi', and typically simmered with leafy greens and meat or fish.
African dishes.Doro wat: Ethiopia's celebrated chicken stew, deeply spiced with berbere and finished with hard-boiled eggs, is traditionally served for holidays.
African dishes.Koshari: Egypt's beloved street food stacks rice, lentils, pasta and chickpeas under spicy tomato sauce and crispy onions, a vegan carb-fest.
African dishes.Ful medames: Slow-cooked fava beans seasoned with olive oil, cumin and lemon; one of the oldest dishes still eaten in Egypt, it's a common breakfast.
African dishes.Chakalaka: A spicy South African relish of peppers, carrots and beans that is said to have started in the Johannesburg mining townships.
African dishes.Feijoada: This black bean and pork stew is the national dish of Brazil, so it belongs to South America, though its roots are tied to Portuguese cooking.
African dishes.Jerk chicken: Spicy with allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers, this is a Jamaican barbecue tradition, not an African dish.
African dishes.Gumbo: Louisiana's stew has West African influence, since the word is thought to come from a Bantu word for okra, but it is an American dish.
African dishes.Ackee and saltfish: Jamaica's national dish pairs salted cod with ackee, a fruit that is poisonous if eaten unripe; it's Caribbean, not African, despite the fruit's West African origin.
African dishes.Mofongo: Fried plantains mashed with garlic and pork cracklings make this Puerto Rican dish, which shows West African influence without being African.
African dishes.Paella: Spain's saffron rice dish started near Valencia, where it's traditionally cooked outdoors over an open fire.
African dishes.Biryani: A layered rice dish of South Asia, famed in Hyderabad and Lucknow, whose name probably comes from Persian.
African dishes.Rendang: This slow-cooked spicy beef dish comes from the Minangkabau people of Sumatra in Indonesia, not Africa.
African dishes.Pupusa: El Salvador's national dish is a thick griddled corn tortilla stuffed with cheese, beans or pork, so it belongs to Central America.
African dishes.Moussaka: Layered eggplant and spiced meat under a creamy béchamel, it's a Greek classic and not African, even though Egypt has similar dishes.
African dishes.Poutine: Quebec's contribution to comfort food is fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, so it's Canadian.

Crustaceans.Crab: Crabs walk sideways because of how their leg joints bend, and many can regrow a lost claw over several molts.
Crustaceans.Lobster: A lobster's blood is clear and turns blue when exposed to air, because it uses copper-based rather than iron-based oxygen carriers.
Crustaceans.Shrimp: A shrimp's heart sits in its head region, just behind the eyes, and the part we eat is mostly its tail muscle.
Crustaceans.Prawn: Prawns and shrimp are close cousins, told apart by gill structure and body shape, but the names are used loosely in different countries.
Crustaceans.Crayfish: Crayfish are freshwater lobster lookalikes; Louisiana boils huge quantities of them, and some species survive out of water in damp burrows.
Crustaceans.Krill: Krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that gather in swarms so large they show up on satellite images and feed the biggest whales.
Crustaceans.Barnacle: Barnacles are crustaceans that spend adult life glued headfirst to rocks or ship hulls, and Charles Darwin studied them for eight years.
Crustaceans.Woodlouse: Woodlice are land-living crustaceans, relatives of crabs, which still breathe with gill-like structures and so need damp places.
Crustaceans.Hermit crab: Hermit crabs borrow empty shells, and sometimes line up by size to swap into each other's in a chain of upgrades.
Crustaceans.Langoustine: Langoustines are small lobster-like crustaceans, also sold as Norway lobster, Dublin Bay prawn or, in cooking, scampi.
Crustaceans.King crab: King crabs can span well over a meter across their legs and are caught in icy Alaskan and Russian waters, famously on 'Deadliest Catch'.
Crustaceans.Horseshoe crab: Trap: despite its name, a horseshoe crab is closer kin to spiders and scorpions, and its blue blood is used to test vaccines for contamination.
Crustaceans.Octopus: Octopuses are shell-less mollusks with three hearts, not crustaceans, even though they hunt crabs with impressive skill.
Crustaceans.Squid: Squid are mollusks, not crustaceans; the giant squid has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, about the size of a dinner plate.
Crustaceans.Clam: Clams are bivalve mollusks, and one ocean quahog nicknamed Ming was about 500 years old when it was found in 2006.
Crustaceans.Oyster: Oysters are mollusks, not crustaceans, and a single oyster can filter dozens of liters of water a day.
Crustaceans.Scallop: Scallops are mollusks that swim by clapping their shells together, and they have rows of tiny eyes along the shell edge.
Crustaceans.Starfish: Starfish are echinoderms, neither fish nor crustaceans, and some species can regrow whole bodies from a single arm.
Crustaceans.Sea urchin: Sea urchins are spiny echinoderms, and their mouth is a five-part chewing apparatus called Aristotle's lantern.
Crustaceans.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are about 95 percent water and have no brain, heart or bones, which puts them nowhere near crustaceans.
Crustaceans.Mussel: Mussels are mollusks that anchor themselves to rocks with tough protein threads that inspired waterproof glues.
Crustaceans.Snail: Snails are mollusks, and a garden snail's tongue-like radula is lined with thousands of tiny teeth.
Crustaceans.Sea cucumber: Sea cucumbers are echinoderms, and when threatened some species expel their internal organs, then regrow them.
Crustaceans.Scorpion: Scorpions are arachnids with eight legs, not crustaceans, and they glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.

Weather instruments.Barometer: It measures air pressure. Falling readings usually warn of storms, which is why old ship captains tapped theirs every day.
Weather instruments.Thermometer: Galileo-era inventors built early versions; Fahrenheit's 1714 mercury model was the first widely trusted for accurate readings.
Weather instruments.Anemometer: Measures wind speed. The classic spinning-cup design was invented in 1846 by Irish astronomer John Thomas Romney Robinson.
Weather instruments.Hygrometer: Measures humidity. The first workable versions used hair, because human hair stretches measurably as moisture rises.
Weather instruments.Rain gauge: One of the oldest weather tools: Korea made standardized bronze ones in the 1440s, well before Europe had them.
Weather instruments.Weather vane: It points the way the wind comes from, not where it goes. A rooster is the classic shape, a tradition from medieval church tops.
Weather instruments.Windsock: The cone shows wind direction and strength at airfields; when it stands fully straight, wind is roughly 15 knots or more.
Weather instruments.Weather balloon: Launched twice daily worldwide, these balloons expand as they climb and burst at about 30 kilometers, dropping their instruments by parachute.
Weather instruments.Doppler radar: Detects the motion of raindrops by frequency shifts, which lets forecasters see a tornado's rotation before it touches down.
Weather instruments.Weather satellite: Orbiting from about 36,000 kilometers up, geostationary satellites watch the same patch of Earth continuously, tracking hurricanes live.
Weather instruments.Seismograph: A trap: it records earthquake vibrations in the ground, so it studies the Earth, not the weather.
Weather instruments.Odometer: Not a weather tool: it counts distance traveled. Roman engineers described such devices on carts over two thousand years ago.
Weather instruments.Speedometer: Measures a vehicle's speed, not weather. The first car versions appeared in the early 1900s, though anemometers are what track wind.
Weather instruments.Stethoscope: A doctor's tool for listening to the body. Laennec invented it in 1816 partly to avoid pressing his ear to a patient's chest.
Weather instruments.Telescope: It looks at the sky but studies space, not weather. Lippershey filed a patent for one in the Netherlands in 1608.
Weather instruments.Pedometer: It counts steps, not weather. Leonardo da Vinci sketched one, and Japan's 10,000-step goal came from a 1960s marketing campaign.
Weather instruments.Sextant: A navigator's tool measuring the angle between a star or the sun and the horizon to find latitude at sea.
Weather instruments.Microscope: Magnifies tiny things, not weather. Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used his to be the first to see bacteria.
Weather instruments.Voltmeter: Measures electrical potential, not weather, though lightning forecasting does use field meters that work on a related principle.
Weather instruments.Geiger counter: Detects radiation, not weather. Its characteristic clicks are the sound of individual particles passing through the tube.
Weather instruments.Periscope: Lets you see around obstacles, famously from a submerged submarine. It has nothing to do with the weather.
Weather instruments.Metronome: A musician's ticking timekeeper, not a weather device. Beethoven was among the first composers to mark tempos with its numbers.
Weather instruments.Kaleidoscope: Scottish physicist David Brewster invented it in 1816. It makes patterns with mirrors and has no weather use.
Weather instruments.Spirometer: Measures how much air your lungs can hold and exhale, so it is a medical device, not a weather instrument.

Types of sushi.Nigiri: Nigiri is a hand-pressed mound of rice with a slice of fish on top, and the name comes from 'nigiru', to grasp.
Types of sushi.Maki: Maki means 'roll', so a maki is seaweed wrapped around rice and fillings, then cut into bite-sized pieces.
Types of sushi.Temaki: Temaki is a hand-roll, a cone of nori filled with rice and fish, and it's meant to be eaten right away before the seaweed softens.
Types of sushi.Uramaki: Uramaki is an 'inside-out' roll, with rice on the outside and nori inside, and it was invented partly to appeal to Western diners.
Types of sushi.Chirashi: Chirashi means 'scattered', and the dish is a bowl of vinegared rice topped with sashimi and garnishes.
Types of sushi.Gunkan: Gunkan means 'battleship', and this sushi is a rice oval wrapped in a strip of nori to hold loose toppings like roe or sea urchin.
Types of sushi.Inari: Inari is rice stuffed in a sweet fried tofu pocket, named after the fox-linked rice god Inari, whose messengers, foxes, are said to love fried tofu.
Types of sushi.Oshizushi: Oshizushi is pressed sushi made in a wooden box mold, a style from Osaka, so it's served in neat blocks.
Types of sushi.California roll: California roll was invented in North America, probably in the 1960s or 70s, to hide the seaweed and use avocado in place of raw fish.
Types of sushi.Futomaki: Futomaki means 'fat roll', a thick roll of nori stuffed with several fillings, and it's often eaten at Setsubun.
Types of sushi.Hosomaki: Hosomaki means 'thin roll', a small nori roll with a single filling, such as cucumber in the kappa maki.
Types of sushi.Sashimi: Sashimi is just sliced raw fish with no rice, which makes it technically not sushi, since sushi refers to the vinegared rice.
Types of sushi.Tempura: Tempura is battered, deep-fried food, and it was introduced to Japan by Portuguese missionaries in the 1500s, so it isn't sushi.
Types of sushi.Gyoza: Gyoza are pan-fried dumplings, derived from Chinese jiaozi, and they're a side dish, not sushi.
Types of sushi.Ramen: Ramen is a noodle soup of Chinese origin that became a Japanese staple, and it has no relation to sushi.
Types of sushi.Edamame: Edamame are boiled soybeans served as a snack, and they're a side dish at sushi restaurants, not sushi.
Types of sushi.Miso soup: Miso soup comes with sushi meals but is a soup, so it doesn't count as a sushi type.
Types of sushi.Wasabi: Wasabi is a condiment served with sushi, and it's not a type of sushi.
Types of sushi.Onigiri: Onigiri are hand-formed rice balls, often wrapped in nori, but they're not vinegared, so they differ from sushi.
Types of sushi.Poke: Poke is a Hawaiian dish of cubed raw fish, usually served over rice, and is a cousin, not a sushi type.
Types of sushi.Bento: Bento is a packed meal in a compartment box, and it can contain sushi, but it's a meal, not a sushi type.
Types of sushi.Yakitori: Yakitori is skewered grilled chicken, from the Japanese for 'grilled bird', and has nothing to do with sushi.
Types of sushi.Takoyaki: Takoyaki are octopus-filled batter balls from Osaka, cooked in a special pan, and aren't sushi.
Types of sushi.Katsu: Katsu is a breaded, fried cutlet, whose name is short for 'katsuretsu', from the English word cutlet, so it is not sushi.

Foods that are usually deep-fried.Tempura: Japanese batter-fried seafood and vegetables, introduced by Portuguese traders in the 1500s. The batter uses ice-cold water to stay crisp.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Doughnut: A ring of dough fried in oil. The hole helps the dough cook evenly, as the center would remain raw otherwise.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.French fries: Often fried twice: first at a low temperature to cook inside, then hot to crisp. The double fry makes them fluffy.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Churros: Spanish ridged dough sticks fried and dusted with sugar. The ridges come from a star-shaped nozzle.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Falafel: Ground chickpea or fava balls fried until crisp. Egypt's version is made with fava beans, called ta'amiya.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Onion rings: Sliced onions in batter fried until golden. They're a diner and pub favorite.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Corn dog: A hot dog dipped in cornmeal batter and fried on a stick. It is popular at American state fairs.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Spring roll: A thin wrapper around vegetables and often meat, fried until crisp. Their name is linked to the spring festival.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Samosa: Triangular fried pastry stuffed with spiced potato and peas. It traveled to India from Central Asia centuries ago.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Calamari: Squid rings in crisp batter. The word is simply Italian for squid.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Funnel cake: Batter poured through a funnel into hot oil in squiggles. It's a fairground classic with Pennsylvania Dutch roots.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Tonkatsu: Japanese breaded pork cutlet fried in panko. Its name combines pork (ton) and cutlet (katsu).
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Hush puppies: Fried cornmeal balls of the American South. One story says cooks tossed them to quiet barking dogs.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Arancini: Sicilian stuffed rice balls, breaded and fried. The name means little oranges.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Sashimi: Raw sliced fish, with no cooking at all. The knife skills matter more than the stove.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Ceviche: Raw fish cured by citrus juice. The acid turns the flesh opaque as if cooked, without heat.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Gazpacho: A cold soup of raw vegetables. Nothing is fried or even heated.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Poached egg: Cooked gently in simmering water. Adding vinegar helps the white set.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Steamed bun: Cooked by steam in a bamboo basket. Fluffy, moist and never fried.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Risotto: Rice stirred slowly in hot stock. Fried only briefly in butter at the start, as the grains are toasted.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Carpaccio: Thinly sliced raw beef, named after the painter Vittore Carpaccio because of the meat's red hues. It's served raw.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Caprese salad: Tomato, mozzarella and basil, which echo the colors of the Italian flag. Nothing is cooked.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Hummus: Cooked chickpeas blended smooth. Only the falafel version of chickpeas gets fried.
Foods that are usually deep-fried.Pho: Vietnamese noodle soup built on a long-simmered broth. Nothing in it is fried.

Sausages.Bratwurst: Germany's pork sausage takes its name from Brät, finely minced meat. Nuremberg's tiny finger-sized version is protected by EU geographical status.
Sausages.Chorizo: Spanish chorizo gets its red colour and smoky bite from pimentón, paprika made from dried peppers, brought to Europe from the Americas.
Sausages.Kielbasa: Poland's smoked garlicky sausage; the word simply means sausage in Polish. Immigrants brought it to America, where it is often just called Polish sausage.
Sausages.Andouille: Smoky Cajun sausage from Louisiana, pork cured with garlic and pepper. It traces back to French and German settlers and flavors classic gumbo and jambalaya.
Sausages.Merguez: Spicy North African lamb or beef sausage coloured red by harissa. It is a favourite grilled street food in Morocco, Tunisia, and in France.
Sausages.Frankfurter: The classic hot dog sausage, named for Frankfurt, Germany. Its American cousin, the wiener, is named after Vienna, which is why the dogs carry two cities' names.
Sausages.Cumberland: A coiled, unlinked pork sausage from Cumbria, England, seasoned with pepper. It has protected status in the EU and is traditionally sold by length, not weight.
Sausages.Boudin: Louisiana's Cajun rice-and-pork sausage, whose name comes from the French for blood sausage, although the usual version today contains no blood.
Sausages.Salami: Italian for 'salted', the word covers many cured sausages. Salami is fermented and air-dried, not cooked, and safe because of salt, acid, and drying.
Sausages.Pepperoni: An American invention, not Italian: the name borrows peperoni, Italian for large peppers. Real Italian pepperoni means peppers, so pizza here means salami.
Sausages.Bockwurst: A German white sausage traditionally served with beer; the name comes from the bock beer once drunk with it. Its pale veal-pork mixture is mild.
Sausages.Black pudding: Neither black nor pudding in the dessert sense: it is blood sausage thickened with oats or barley. Eaten for breakfast in Britain and Ireland for centuries.
Sausages.Mortadella: Bologna's pride is a huge, smooth pork sausage studded with fat cubes and pistachios. American bologna is named after it, but the original is far fancier.
Sausages.Lap cheong: Chinese dried pork sausage, sweet and slightly boozy from rice wine. It is steamed with rice and often eaten at Lunar New Year.
Sausages.Prosciutto: A trap: prosciutto is a whole cured ham leg, dry-cured and sliced thin, not minced and stuffed into a casing like sausage. Parma's is the most famous.
Sausages.Pancetta: Italian cured pork belly, salted and spiced and rolled into a log. It is meat from a cut, not ground and stuffed, so it is not a sausage.
Sausages.Bacon: Cured, smoked pork belly sold in strips. It is whole-cut meat rather than ground and stuffed, though breakfast sausage often sits right beside it.
Sausages.Ham: A cured or cooked hind leg of pork, not ground and encased. Spain's jamon iberico from acorn-fed pigs can cost hundreds of dollars a leg.
Sausages.Jerky: Dried strips of meat, not ground and stuffed in a casing. The word comes from the Quechua ch'arki, meaning dried meat.
Sausages.Pastrami: Beef brisket brined with spices, smoked, and steamed; New York deli staple. It came with Romanian Jewish immigrants and is sliced, not stuffed like sausage.
Sausages.Bresaola: Italian air-dried salted beef, aged for months until dark and tender. It is a whole muscle, so it is a cured meat and not a sausage.
Sausages.Biltong: South African dried cured meat, a cousin of jerky but spiced with coriander and vinegar. It is a whole cut, so no sausage; its stick cousin is called droewors.
Sausages.Meatball: A ball of ground meat, so close to a sausage in the mix, but never in a casing. Swedish meatballs gained world fame through a certain furniture store's cafeteria.
Sausages.Corned beef: Salt-cured beef brisket, named for the large grains of 'corns' of salt once used. A whole cut of meat, not ground and stuffed into casing like a sausage.

US state capitals.Sacramento: California's capital, a Gold Rush supply town. The state's big cities are bigger, but the capital is here.
US state capitals.Albany: New York's capital is not New York City, and has been the capital since 1797. It's one of the oldest in the US.
US state capitals.Austin: The Texas capital, and Houston is larger. It calls itself the Live Music Capital of the World.
US state capitals.Tallahassee: Florida's capital, chosen in 1824 as the midway point between St. Augustine and Pensacola. Miami is far larger.
US state capitals.Springfield: Illinois's capital, where Abraham Lincoln lived before the presidency. Chicago is much larger, but not the capital.
US state capitals.Harrisburg: Pennsylvania's capital, not Philadelphia or Pittsburgh. It sits on the Susquehanna River, and its small size surprises visitors.
US state capitals.Olympia: Washington's capital, a small city on Puget Sound, not Seattle. It is named for a local Native word.
US state capitals.Boise: Idaho's capital and largest city, whose name comes from French 'boisé', 'wooded', for the trees along the river.
US state capitals.Juneau: Alaska's capital, which can only be reached by air or sea, with no road connecting it to the rest of the state.
US state capitals.Honolulu: The capital of Hawaii, on Oahu. The name means 'sheltered bay', and it's the state's largest city.
US state capitals.Denver: Colorado's capital, nicknamed the Mile High City, as its official elevation is exactly 5,280 feet.
US state capitals.Boston: Massachusetts's capital since 1630, one of the oldest US cities. The Boston Tea Party of 1773 happened in its harbour.
US state capitals.Atlanta: Georgia's capital and largest city, a major airport hub, and it replaced Milledgeville in 1868.
US state capitals.Los Angeles: A trap: California's biggest city and the film capital, but Sacramento is the state capital.
US state capitals.New York City: A trap: the largest US city, but the capital of New York state is Albany, about 240 km upriver.
US state capitals.Houston: A trap: Texas's largest city and home of NASA's Mission Control, but Austin is the capital.
US state capitals.Miami: A trap: Florida's best-known city, but Tallahassee, in the northern panhandle, is the capital.
US state capitals.Chicago: A trap: Illinois's giant, the country's third-largest city, but Springfield, Lincoln's hometown, is the capital.
US state capitals.Philadelphia: A trap: Pennsylvania's largest city and the early national capital, but Harrisburg is the state capital.
US state capitals.Seattle: A trap: Washington state's biggest city, but the capital is Olympia, about 100 km south.
US state capitals.Portland: A trap: Oregon's largest city, but the capital is Salem, to the south. Maine has a Portland too, not its capital either.
US state capitals.Las Vegas: A trap: Nevada's largest city, but the capital is the small city of Carson City.
US state capitals.Dallas: A trap: a large Texas city, but not the capital, which is Austin.
US state capitals.Detroit: A trap: Michigan's largest city and the home of the car industry, but the capital is Lansing.

Big cities that are not national capital.Sydney: Australia's largest city, not its capital; Canberra was purpose-built in 1913 as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne.
Big cities that are not national capital.Toronto: Canada's biggest city is not the capital, and over half its residents were born outside the country, making it very diverse.
Big cities that are not national capital.New York: The most populous US city has never been the national capital for long, though it hosted the first Congress in 1789.
Big cities that are not national capital.Istanbul: Straddles Europe and Asia and was capital of Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires, but Atatürk moved Turkey's capital to Ankara in 1923.
Big cities that are not national capital.Shanghai: China's largest city by population and its financial hub, with the world's busiest container port, though Beijing is the capital.
Big cities that are not national capital.Mumbai: India's financial capital and home of Bollywood, built on seven islands later joined by land reclamation.
Big cities that are not national capital.Rio de Janeiro: Brazil's capital until 1960, when the government moved to the newly built Brasília, still its famed beach city.
Big cities that are not national capital.Zurich: Switzerland's biggest city and a banking centre, but the capital is Bern, which formally is just a federal city.
Big cities that are not national capital.Los Angeles: The second-largest US city, with a name meaning The Angels, and the home of Hollywood.
Big cities that are not national capital.Lagos: Nigeria's largest city, a huge port of over 15 million, was its capital until 1991, when Abuja replaced it.
Big cities that are not national capital.Karachi: Pakistan's largest city and port, and its first capital until 1959, then Islamabad took over.
Big cities that are not national capital.Johannesburg: South Africa's biggest city, born in an 1886 gold rush, but the country has three capitals and Johannesburg is none of them.
Big cities that are not national capital.Auckland: New Zealand's largest city, sitting on a volcanic field with about 50 dormant cones, while Wellington is the capital.
Big cities that are not national capital.Canberra: Australia's capital was designed by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin after a design competition.
Big cities that are not national capital.Ottawa: Canada's capital was picked by Queen Victoria in 1857, partly because it lay between English and French regions.
Big cities that are not national capital.Ankara: Turkey's capital since 1923, replacing Istanbul, chosen partly for its safe interior position.
Big cities that are not national capital.Beijing: A trap: it is China's capital, so it fails the subject; the city has been a capital for most of the past 800 years.
Big cities that are not national capital.New Delhi: India's capital, designed by Edwin Lutyens and inaugurated in 1931, built next to the old city of Delhi.
Big cities that are not national capital.Brasília: Brazil's capital was built from scratch in the 1950s, inaugurated in 1960, with a plan shaped like an airplane.
Big cities that are not national capital.Bern: The Swiss capital, with a medieval centre, a bear-pit mascot and the Zytglogge clock tower.
Big cities that are not national capital.Wellington: New Zealand's capital is among the windiest big cities and the world's southernmost national capital.
Big cities that are not national capital.Abuja: Nigeria's capital, purpose-built in the 1980s in the centre of the country, replaced Lagos in 1991.
Big cities that are not national capital.Islamabad: Pakistan's planned capital from the 1960s sits at the foot of the Margalla Hills, and replaced Karachi.
The US capital, named for George Washington, and it isn't part of any state, but is a federal district.

States on the Appalachian Trail.Georgia: The trail's southern end is on Springer Mountain, where a bronze plaque marks mile zero and many hikers begin the roughly 2,200 mile walk.
States on the Appalachian Trail.North Carolina: The trail wanders along the Tennessee line here and crosses the Great Smoky Mountains, reaching its highest point at Clingmans Dome.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Tennessee: The trail follows the Tennessee and North Carolina border for hundreds of miles, and it goes over the highest point at Clingmans Dome.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Virginia: It holds more miles of the trail than any other state, about a quarter of the total, and the trail passes the Shenandoah National Park.
States on the Appalachian Trail.West Virginia: It has the shortest trail section by far at about four miles, though Harpers Ferry, the trail's spiritual midpoint, is right here.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Maryland: The trail runs about 40 miles along South Mountain, and Maryland is where hikers cross the Mason-Dixon line.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Pennsylvania: Known for sharp rocks called Rocksylvania, which wear out the boots of long-distance hikers.
States on the Appalachian Trail.New Jersey: The trail crosses the state in about 70 miles, within an hour of New York City, and you may meet black bears.
States on the Appalachian Trail.New York: A short stretch at about 90 miles, it includes a train station near the trail, the only one on the entire route.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Connecticut: The path follows the Housatonic River valley, and passes through about 50 miles of woods and ridgeline.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Massachusetts: The trail goes over Mount Greylock, the state's highest point, and through the Berkshires.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Vermont: Here the trail overlaps the Long Trail, the oldest long-distance hiking path in the US.
States on the Appalachian Trail.New Hampshire: The White Mountains are the toughest section, and Mount Washington nearby is known for severe weather.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Maine: The trail ends at Katahdin, where hikers climb the final Baxter Peak, after the notoriously remote 100-Mile Wilderness.
States on the Appalachian Trail.South Carolina: Trap: the trail brushes past it near the Georgia line but never enters; the Foothills Trail is South Carolina's own long mountain path.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Kentucky: Trap: Kentucky has Appalachian hills in the east, but the trail runs farther east, through Virginia and West Virginia instead.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Ohio: Ohio lies west of the Appalachian chain's main ridges; the trail stays in the eastern states, and Ohio has its own Buckeye Trail loop.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Delaware: Delaware is one of the flattest states, with a high point of only about 135 meters, so the trail passes it by on its way north.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Rhode Island: Trap: the trail goes through Connecticut and Massachusetts but skips Rhode Island, which sits just east of the route.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Alabama: The Appalachian mountains do fade out in Alabama, but the trail starts in Georgia, leaving Alabama off the list.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Florida: Florida has its own long path, the Florida Trail, and it is far from the trail, which is a long way north.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Indiana: Indiana is a mostly flat Midwestern state, with no Appalachian ridges, and the trail never goes near it.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Michigan: Michigan has the North Country Trail instead, and the Appalachian Trail never reaches the Great Lakes.
States on the Appalachian Trail.Illinois: Illinois is prairie country far from the trail, which stays within the Appalachian ridges of the East.

Muscles or muscle groups.Biceps: The name means two heads in Latin. It is better at turning the forearm, as in screwing a screw, than many people realize.
Muscles or muscle groups.Triceps: With three heads, it forms about two thirds of the upper arm and straightens the elbow. Many people forget it, but it is the bigger arm muscle.
Muscles or muscle groups.Deltoid: The rounded shoulder muscle is named for the Greek letter delta, because of its triangular shape.
Muscles or muscle groups.Quadriceps: This four-part muscle group at the front of the thigh includes the rectus femoris and is the largest muscle mass in the body.
Muscles or muscle groups.Hamstrings: The three muscles along the back of the thigh. Their name comes from butchers, who hung hams by these tendons.
Muscles or muscle groups.Gluteus maximus: The largest muscle in the human body by mass. It helps you stand upright and climb stairs.
Muscles or muscle groups.Pectoralis major: The big fan-shaped chest muscle. It pulls the arm across the body and is what bench presses train.
Muscles or muscle groups.Diaphragm: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs. It does most of the work of breathing, and hiccups are its spasms.
Muscles or muscle groups.Trapezius: A large diamond-shaped muscle across the upper back and neck, named after the trapezoid. It moves your shoulder blades.
Muscles or muscle groups.Latissimus dorsi: A broad back muscle nicknamed the lats. It gives swimmers their V shape and powers pull-ups.
Muscles or muscle groups.Rectus abdominis: The muscle behind the six-pack. Everyone has them, but they are visible only when body fat is low.
Muscles or muscle groups.Femur: A trap: it's the thigh bone, not an organ of the abdomen. It is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
Muscles or muscle groups.Humerus: A trap: it's the upper arm bone, not a muscle. Hitting its nerve at the elbow gives you the funny bone feeling.
Muscles or muscle groups.Tendon: A trap: tendons attach muscle to bone, but are not muscle. They are made of tough collagen and can't contract.
Muscles or muscle groups.Ligament: A trap: it connects bone to bone, not a muscle. It has little stretch, so sprains are slow to heal.
Muscles or muscle groups.Patella: A trap: it's the kneecap, a bone. It sits inside the quadriceps tendon, acting as a pulley.
Muscles or muscle groups.Clavicle: A trap: it's the collarbone, not a muscle. It is the bone most often broken in childhood falls.
Muscles or muscle groups.Sternum: A trap: the breastbone, not a muscle. Several ribs connect to it through cartilage.
Muscles or muscle groups.Scapula: A trap: the shoulder blade, a bone. Many muscles attach to it, but it is not a muscle.
Muscles or muscle groups.Cartilage: A trap: smooth flexible tissue, neither bone nor muscle. It has no blood supply, so it heals slowly.
Muscles or muscle groups.Spleen: A trap: it's an organ in the upper left abdomen, not a muscle. It filters blood.
Muscles or muscle groups.Retina: A trap: the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, not muscle. It has about 120 million rod cells for dim light.
Muscles or muscle groups.Tibia: A trap: it's the shinbone, not a muscle. It's the second-largest bone in the body.
Muscles or muscle groups.Larynx: A trap: the voice box, an organ made of cartilage and muscle, not a muscle itself. The Adam's apple is part of it.

Things a meteorologist studies.Clouds: Classified by Luke Howard in 1802 with Latin names like cumulus and cirrus, which are still used by forecasters today.
Things a meteorologist studies.Rain: Raindrops are not tear-shaped; small ones are spheres and larger ones flatten like hamburger buns as they fall.
Things a meteorologist studies.Hurricanes: A mature one can release heat energy equal to hundreds of times the world's electricity generating capacity.
Things a meteorologist studies.Tornadoes: The Enhanced Fujita scale rates them EF0 to EF5 by damage caused, since measuring wind inside a tornado is so hard.
Things a meteorologist studies.Humidity: Why a hot day feels worse when it's muggy: sweat evaporates slowly into moist air, so your body cools less effectively.
Things a meteorologist studies.Air pressure: Falling pressure usually signals stormy weather ahead, which is why old barometers were marked with words like Rain and Fair.
Things a meteorologist studies.Wind: The Beaufort scale, devised in 1805 for sailors, rates wind from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force) by its visible effects.
Things a meteorologist studies.Snow: Every flake forms around a speck of dust, and its six-sided shape comes from the way water molecules bond when freezing.
Things a meteorologist studies.Hail: Stones grow in layers as storm updrafts toss them up and down, and the heaviest recorded in the US weighed nearly 1 kg.
Things a meteorologist studies.Fog: It's simply a cloud touching the ground, made of tiny water droplets that form when air cools to its dew point.
Things a meteorologist studies.Lightning: A bolt is hotter than the surface of the Sun, about 30,000 degrees C, and strikes Earth roughly 100 times each second.
Things a meteorologist studies.Jet stream: These fast river-like winds high up can exceed 400 km/h, and airlines ride them to shorten eastbound flights.
Things a meteorologist studies.Dew: Not rain: it forms when surfaces cool overnight below the dew point, and water vapor condenses on grass and leaves.
Things a meteorologist studies.Meteors: A trap: despite the name, meteorology does not study these shooting stars; it focuses on weather, from the Greek for things high in the sky.
Things a meteorologist studies.Comets: A trap: icy visitors from space belong to astronomy; meteorologists study only what happens inside our atmosphere.
Things a meteorologist studies.Earthquakes: A trap: these belong to seismologists. Weather scientists only care about quakes if, say, a tsunami follows.
Things a meteorologist studies.Volcanoes: A trap: volcanology is its own science, though big eruptions do affect weather; Tambora in 1815 caused a year without a summer.
Things a meteorologist studies.Fossils: A trap: these are paleontology's business; meteorologists look at air, not rock.
Things a meteorologist studies.Asteroids: A trap: space rocks are studied by astronomers and planetary scientists, not by weather forecasters.
Things a meteorologist studies.Tides: A trap: tides come from the Moon's and Sun's gravity, so they fall under oceanography, even though storms can alter water levels.
Things a meteorologist studies.Plate tectonics: A trap: this slow shifting of Earth's crust is geology, working over millions of years, not weather's daily timescale.
Things a meteorologist studies.Tsunamis: A trap: tsunamis are caused by undersea quakes or landslides, not wind, so they are not weather, despite sounding like it.
Things a meteorologist studies.Planets: A trap: planets belong to astronomy, though meteorologists do study atmospheres on Mars and Venus as comparisons.
Things a meteorologist studies.Black holes: A trap: far beyond Earth's atmosphere, these are the territory of astrophysicists, not forecasters.

Landforms carved by glaciers.Fjord: A glacier-carved valley later flooded by the sea. Norway's Sognefjord is about 1,300 meters deep.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Moraine: A ridge or pile of rock and debris pushed along and dropped by a glacier. Long Island, New York, is largely made of moraines.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Drumlin: A smooth, oval hill shaped like an upside-down spoon, molded under moving ice. They often appear in swarms of hundreds.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Cirque: A bowl-shaped hollow on a mountainside, carved at the head of a glacier. Many hold a small lake after the ice melts.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Arete: A sharp, knife-edge ridge left between two glacial cirques. The word is French for fishbone or ridge.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Esker: A long, winding ridge of sand and gravel, deposited by a stream flowing inside or under a glacier. Some run for hundreds of kilometers.
Landforms carved by glaciers.U-shaped valley: Glaciers carve valleys with steep walls and flat floors, unlike the V-shape of river valleys. Yosemite Valley is a famous example.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Kettle lake: Formed when a buried block of ice melts and leaves a hollow. Thousands of them dot parts of Minnesota and Wisconsin.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Erratic: A boulder carried far from its source and dumped by ice, often sitting on totally different rock. Some are the size of houses.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Horn: A pyramid-shaped peak sculpted by several cirques eating into it. The Matterhorn is the classic example.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Tarn: A small mountain lake in a cirque left by a glacier. The word comes from Old Norse for a small lake.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Delta: Built by rivers depositing sediment at their mouth. Water and sand, not ice, shape it.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Oxbow lake: A crescent-shaped lake that forms when a river meander is cut off. It's a river feature.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Mesa: A flat-topped hill formed by erosion in dry regions. Wind and water cut it, not ice.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Butte: A narrow, steep hill left by erosion in arid lands. It forms without glaciers.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Sand dune: A mound of sand piled up by wind. Deserts and coasts produce them, and not ice.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Atoll: A coral ring forming around a sunken volcano. It comes from marine life and not glaciers.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Volcano: A mountain built by erupting magma. It's an internal Earth feature, though glaciers can sit on top of one.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Sinkhole: A hole formed when the ground collapses into dissolved rock below. Water, not ice, causes it.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Hoodoo: A slim rock pillar sculpted by wind and rain, with frost playing a part in the process. Glaciers aren't responsible.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Geyser: Hot water and steam erupting from the ground. It's volcanic heat, not glacial.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Stalactite: A mineral icicle hanging in caves, with no true ice involved. Dripping water builds it, not a glacier.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Barrier island: A long sandy island parallel to the coast, built by waves and currents. It forms by ocean action, not glaciers.
Landforms carved by glaciers.Sea stack: A tower of rock left when waves erode a headland. It's carved by the sea.

Inventions from ancient China.Paper: Traditionally credited to Cai Lun in AD 105, though fragments of earlier paper have been found.
Inventions from ancient China.Gunpowder: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of immortality stumbled on it around the 9th century.
Inventions from ancient China.Magnetic compass: Early ones were fortune-telling tools using lodestone, and sailors used them later.
Inventions from ancient China.Woodblock printing: The oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra of AD 868, was printed this way.
Inventions from ancient China.Silk: Legend credits Empress Leizu, who supposedly found it when a cocoon dropped in her tea, and China guarded the secret for thousands of years.
Inventions from ancient China.Porcelain: So tied to China that English calls tableware 'china', though the word porcelain itself comes from Italian.
Inventions from ancient China.Seismoscope: Zhang Heng built one in AD 132 where a bronze dragon dropped a ball to show the direction of a distant quake.
Inventions from ancient China.Paper money: Used in China by the Song dynasty, centuries before Europe printed any.
Inventions from ancient China.Fireworks: Born from bamboo stalks thrown on fires that popped loudly to scare off evil spirits, and later joined with gunpowder.
Inventions from ancient China.Toilet paper: Documented in China by the 6th century AD, and later made for the imperial court in huge quantity.
Inventions from ancient China.Chopsticks: Used for over 3,000 years, perhaps starting as cooking tools.
Inventions from ancient China.Telescope: Invented in the Netherlands around 1608, and Galileo improved it the next year.
Inventions from ancient China.Printing press: A trap: China had movable type around 1040, but the mechanical press is Gutenberg's of the 1440s.
Inventions from ancient China.Steam engine: Hero of Alexandria's toy engine came first, but practical engines came with Newcomen in 1712 and Watt later.
Inventions from ancient China.Pendulum clock: Huygens built the first in 1656, though Su Song's giant water clock tower in China dates to 1090.
Inventions from ancient China.Telephone: Patented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, though Elisha Gray filed the same day, and Meucci also made claims.
Inventions from ancient China.Light bulb: Many inventors worked on it; Swan in Britain and Edison in America both produced practical lamps in the 1870s.
Inventions from ancient China.Microscope: Dutch lens-makers developed compound microscopes around 1600, and Leeuwenhoek later used one to be first to see bacteria.
Inventions from ancient China.Eyeglasses: Spectacle lenses were made in Italy around the 1280s.
Inventions from ancient China.Thermometer: Galileo's 1600 thermoscope came first, but Fahrenheit's mercury version came in 1714.
Inventions from ancient China.Airplane: A trap: China invented the kite, an early flying machine, but the powered plane is the Wright brothers' 1903.
Inventions from ancient China.Barometer: Torricelli made the first one in Italy in 1643.
Inventions from ancient China.Television: Developed in the 1920s by Baird, Farnsworth and others.
Inventions from ancient China.Bicycle: Karl von Drais built a pedal-less one in Germany in 1817, and pedals came decades later.

James Bond film titles.Goldfinger: The 1964 film made the Aston Martin DB5 famous, and Shirley Bassey's theme set the template for later Bond songs.
James Bond film titles.Skyfall: Adele's title song won the Oscar for Best Original Song, and the 2012 film is Bond's highest-grossing release.
James Bond film titles.Dr. No: The 1962 film began the series, with Sean Connery's famous introduction, 'Bond, James Bond'.
James Bond film titles.Thunderball: The 1965 film features a famous underwater battle, and it was one of the series' most expensive early productions.
James Bond film titles.Moonraker: The 1979 film sent Roger Moore's Bond into space, riding the wave of Star Wars's success.
James Bond film titles.GoldenEye: Pierce Brosnan's debut in 1995 takes its name from Ian Fleming's Jamaican estate, where he wrote the Bond novels.
James Bond film titles.Spectre: The 2015 film opens with a long tracking shot in Mexico City's Day of the Dead parade.
James Bond film titles.Casino Royale: Daniel Craig's 2006 debut adapts Fleming's first Bond novel, from 1953, and rebooted the series.
James Bond film titles.Live and Let Die: Paul McCartney and Wings recorded the theme to Roger Moore's 1973 debut, and it earned an Oscar nomination.
James Bond film titles.Quantum of Solace: This 2008 film is the shortest Bond film, at around 106 minutes, and continues straight from Casino Royale.
James Bond film titles.No Time to Die: Daniel Craig's final Bond film, from 2021, was delayed repeatedly by the pandemic before release.
James Bond film titles.Licence to Kill: Timothy Dalton's 1989 film was retitled from 'Licence Revoked' late on, reportedly because many Americans might not know the word 'revoked'.
James Bond film titles.Die Another Day: The 2002 film marked Bond's 40th anniversary and was Pierce Brosnan's last turn as 007.
James Bond film titles.Kingsman: The Kingsman films are a spy parody from Matthew Vaughn, and aren't part of the Bond series.
James Bond film titles.Salt: Angelina Jolie's spy thriller from 2010 isn't a Bond film.
James Bond film titles.Taken: Liam Neeson's 2008 revenge thriller isn't Bond, though it's a spy-adjacent action film.
James Bond film titles.Atomic Blonde: Charlize Theron's 2017 Cold War spy film isn't a Bond movie, though it shares a thriller style.
James Bond film titles.True Lies: Arnold Schwarzenegger's 1994 spy comedy isn't a Bond film.
James Bond film titles.The Bourne Identity: Matt Damon's amnesiac assassin is a rival franchise, not Bond.
James Bond film titles.Spy Game: Robert Redford and Brad Pitt's 2001 CIA thriller isn't Bond.
James Bond film titles.Red Sparrow: Jennifer Lawrence plays a Russian spy in this 2018 film, which isn't Bond.
James Bond film titles.Johnny English: Rowan Atkinson's bumbling spy is a Bond parody, not an actual Bond film.
James Bond film titles.Goldmember: Austin Powers in Goldmember (2002) spoofs Goldfinger, and its title is a trap but not a real Bond film.
James Bond film titles.Charlie's Angels: The detective franchise about three women isn't Bond, though its spy-action tone is similar.

Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Belle: Belle means 'beautiful' in French, and the 1991 film became the first animated feature nominated for the Best Picture Oscar.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.The Beast: The Beast's design blends several animals, including a buffalo's head, a gorilla's brow and a boar's tusks.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Gaston: Gaston is a rare Disney villain with no magic, only ego and a talent for eating five dozen eggs.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.LeFou: LeFou means 'the fool' or 'the madman' in French, and he is Gaston's adoring sidekick who sings his praises.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Lumiere: Lumiere is a candelabra, and his name is French for 'light'. Jerry Orbach, later of Law and Order, voiced him.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Cogsworth: A stiff mantel clock, Cogsworth was voiced by David Ogden Stiers, who also voiced Governor Ratcliffe in Pocahontas.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Mrs. Potts: Angela Lansbury voiced Mrs. Potts and sang the title song, which won the Oscar for Best Original Song.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Chip: Chip, a chipped teacup, is a Disney invention, since the original French fairy tale has no talking household objects.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Maurice: Belle's father is an eccentric inventor in the film, but in the original fairy tale he is a merchant.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Philippe: Philippe is a stout draft horse, and breeds like the Percheron can weigh nearly a ton, as much as a small car.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Prince Eric: Eric is the prince of The Little Mermaid. The Beast's princely name is never spoken in the 1991 film.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Prince Phillip: Phillip is Sleeping Beauty's prince, who defeats Maleficent when she turns into a dragon, using the Sword of Truth.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Prince Charming: Cinderella's prince is simply called 'the Prince' in the film. 'Charming' comes from sequels and merchandise.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Aurora: Sleeping Beauty's Aurora has under 20 minutes of screen time, the least of any title princess in Disney animation.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Flora: Flora is the red-clad leader of Sleeping Beauty's three good fairies, and she is also the bossiest.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Fauna: Fauna, the green fairy of Sleeping Beauty, loves animals, and her name is the Latin word for the animals of a region.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Merryweather: Blue-clad Merryweather is the fiery fairy who argues with Flora over whether Aurora's dress should be pink or blue.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Sebastian: Sebastian belongs to The Little Mermaid. Alan Menken composed both that film's songs and Beauty and the Beast's.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Jiminy Cricket: Pinocchio's conscience is a 1940 Disney creation. In Collodi's book, Pinocchio squashes the Talking Cricket.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Tinker Bell: Her name comes from tinkers, who mended pots and pans, and in J. M. Barrie's play she speaks in bell tinkles.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Fairy Godmother: Cinderella's Fairy Godmother and her 'Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo' magic belong to a different film from Beauty and the Beast.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Pinocchio: Pinocchio comes from Carlo Collodi's Italian novel of 1883, and Disney's 1940 film was only its second animated feature.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Gus Gus: Gus is the chubby, cheese-loving mouse of Cinderella, and his friend Jaq is the clever one.
Characters in Beauty and the Beast.Ursula: The sea witch Ursula of The Little Mermaid was reportedly inspired by drag performer Divine.

Skateboard tricks.900: Tony Hawk landed the first one in 1999 at the X Games after many failed tries, spinning two and a half rotations.
Skateboard tricks.Ollie: Alan Gelfand invented it in Florida in 1978, and it's the base of almost every flip trick in skating.
Skateboard tricks.Kickflip: Rodney Mullen helped popularize the kickflip, where a flick of the foot makes the board spin along its length.
Skateboard tricks.Heelflip: This is the kickflip's mirror, with the heel flicking the board to spin it the other way.
Skateboard tricks.Grind: Skaters slide along edges or rails on their trucks, the metal axles under the board, which is why trucks wear down.
Skateboard tricks.Manual: This trick is a balancing act like a wheelie, rolling on only two wheels, and it's a base for many tricks.
Skateboard tricks.Shove-it: The board spins 180 degrees under the feet while the rider stays facing forward, a relatively simple trick.
Skateboard tricks.Boardslide: The skater slides the middle of the board along a rail or ledge, with the board crossways.
Skateboard tricks.Nollie: A nollie is done by popping off the nose instead of the tail, like an ollie but in reverse.
Skateboard tricks.Tre flip: A combination of a 360 shove-it and a kickflip, this trick was first landed by Rodney Mullen.
Skateboard tricks.Slam dunk: This basketball dunk is a very different jump, and has no place in skateboarding.
Skateboard tricks.Alley-oop: In basketball it's a pass for a dunk, but in skateboarding it's a halfpipe trick, so a sneaky trap.
Skateboard tricks.Triple axel: Figure skaters do this jump with three and a half rotations, a trick far above any skateboard trick.
Skateboard tricks.Lutz: Named for Alois Lutz, it's a figure skating jump taken off from the back outside edge, and nothing like a skateboard trick.
Skateboard tricks.Salchow: Ulrich Salchow, a Swedish skater who won ten world titles, performed the first jump named after him in 1909.
Skateboard tricks.Toe loop: A figure skating jump with a toe pick assist, and it's a skating trick that needs ice, not a skate park.
Skateboard tricks.Handspring: Gymnasts do this by springing from hands to feet, and it's not a skateboard trick.
Skateboard tricks.Cartwheel: A cartwheel is a gymnast's sideways rotation, and it has no relation to the board.
Skateboard tricks.Moonwalk: Michael Jackson made this backward glide famous, though the move is older than he is; it's a dance move, not a trick on a board.
Skateboard tricks.Dab: The dab became a dance craze through hip-hop and athletes, but it's not a skate trick.
Skateboard tricks.Floss: The floss dance was popularized by a teen known as Backpack Kid, and has nothing to do with skate parks.
Skateboard tricks.Butterfly: A swimming stroke named for the way arms sweep like wings; it's also a gymnastics skill, but not a skate trick.
Skateboard tricks.Bicycle kick: In soccer, an overhead kick is a dramatic scoring move that has nothing to do with skating.
Skateboard tricks.Hail Mary: A Hail Mary is a desperation long pass in American football, and has no skateboard link.

Poker terms.Bluff: To bluff is to bet big with a weak hand so others fold, and the skill is in making it believable.
Poker terms.Ante: From Latin for 'before', an ante is a small forced bet from every player before the deal.
Poker terms.Blinds: These are forced bets posted by the two players left of the dealer button, rotating around the table each hand.
Poker terms.Fold: Throwing your hand away and giving up the pot, which is a skill as essential as any bluff.
Poker terms.Raise: Raising increases the bet, making other players pay more to stay in the hand.
Poker terms.River: The river is the fifth and final community card in Texas hold'em.
Poker terms.Flop: The flop is the first three community cards, dealt at once after the first betting round.
Poker terms.Turn: The turn is the fourth community card, also called fourth street.
Poker terms.All in: Going all in means betting every chip, so others must call or fold, and a player can't be forced out of a hand.
Poker terms.Showdown: The final showing of hands decides who wins the pot after the last betting round.
Poker terms.Pot: The pot is the pile of chips in the middle, which the winner takes.
Poker terms.Kicker: The kicker is the unpaired side card that breaks ties between hands that hold the same pair.
Poker terms.Muck: To muck is to discard a hand face-down without showing it, and the muck is also the pile of discarded cards.
Poker terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is the chess finish when the king is trapped, and has no place at the poker table.
Poker terms.Strike: A strike in bowling means knocking down all ten pins with the first ball.
Poker terms.Birdie: A birdie is one under par in golf, a good score that fits no poker table.
Poker terms.Yahtzee: Yahtzee is a dice game with a five-of-a-kind jackpot, but it uses no cards.
Poker terms.Bingo: Bingo is a game of numbered squares and called numbers, where players shout when a line is complete.
Poker terms.Rook: A rook is a chess piece that moves in straight lines, and it castles with the king.
Poker terms.Gambit: A gambit is a chess opening in which a player sacrifices material for position.
Poker terms.Gin: Gin is a rummy card game, not poker, and also a spirit; the card game needs no flop.
Poker terms.Uno: Uno is a shedding card game whose name means 'one' in Spanish, and players must call it when down to one card.
Poker terms.Bullseye: A bullseye is the center of a dartboard, worth 50 points, which has no poker role.
Poker terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is a six-point scoring play in American football, nothing to do with cards.

Skiing terms.Moguls: Moguls are bumps formed when skiers turn repeatedly on the same line, and mogul skiing became an Olympic medal event in 1992.
Skiing terms.Slalom: Slalom is a race down a course of gates, and the word comes from Norwegian 'slalåm', meaning sloping track.
Skiing terms.Piste: Piste is the French word for a marked and groomed ski run, and it's the usual term in Europe for trails.
Skiing terms.Chairlift: Chairlifts carry skiers up the mountain, and the first was built in 1936 at Sun Valley, Idaho.
Skiing terms.Apres-ski: Après-ski is French for 'after skiing', the social time of drinks and music after a day on the slopes.
Skiing terms.Black diamond: A black diamond marks an expert trail in North America, and double black diamonds are harder still.
Skiing terms.Bunny slope: The bunny slope is the gentle beginner hill, where people learn to turn and stop.
Skiing terms.Off-piste: Off-piste means skiing outside marked runs, where avalanches are a risk, and it requires care.
Skiing terms.Gondola: A gondola is an enclosed cabin lift that carries skiers up the mountain.
Skiing terms.Powder: Powder is fresh, light snow that skiers prize, and the best is said to be very dry and deep.
Skiing terms.Schuss: A schuss is skiing straight down the slope, as fast as possible, without turning, from the German word for a shot.
Skiing terms.T-bar: A T-bar is a lift that drags skiers uphill on a T-shaped pole, two at a time.
Skiing terms.Hang ten: Hang ten is a surfing move, where the rider curls all ten toes over the nose of the board, and it needs a longboard and a wave.
Skiing terms.Riptide: A riptide is a strong narrow current flowing out from the shore, a hazard for swimmers, and it has nothing to do with snow.
Skiing terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's three stumps, and the word also names the ground that the bowlers aim at, so it's unrelated to snow.
Skiing terms.Dugout: A dugout is the sunken bench where baseball players sit, and the name comes from it being dug into the ground.
Skiing terms.Bullpen: The bullpen is where baseball relief pitchers warm up, and some say the name comes from a pen where cattle waited.
Skiing terms.Fairway: A fairway is the closely mown grass between the tee and the green on a golf hole, not a ski term.
Skiing terms.Putt: A putt is a gentle golf stroke on the green, aimed at the cup, and has no connection to skiing.
Skiing terms.Lineout: A lineout is a rugby restart where a hooker throws the ball in between two lines of forwards, with jumpers lifted by teammates.
Skiing terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is the bowling mistake of rolling into the side channel, scoring nothing, and the term has no ski meaning.
Skiing terms.Scrum: A scrum is a rugby formation where the forwards bind together and push for the ball, and it's not ski terminology.
Skiing terms.Penalty kick: A penalty kick is a soccer free shot from 12 yards, taken against only the goalkeeper, and it doesn't belong on the slopes.
Skiing terms.Home run: A home run is a baseball hit that clears the outfield fence, and it lets the batter circle all the bases.

Board games that use dice.Monopoly: Rolling doubles three times in a row sends you straight to jail, and Jail is statistically the square players land on most often.
Board games that use dice.Backgammon: One of the oldest known board games, with ancestors some 5,000 years old. The doubling cube was added in 1920s New York.
Board games that use dice.Risk: Battles are settled by dice: attackers roll up to three, defenders up to two, and the highest numbers win. Albert Lamorisse invented it in France.
Board games that use dice.Catan: A dice roll decides which hexes pay out. The 6 and 8 are printed in red because, after 7, they are the likeliest numbers to come up.
Board games that use dice.Trivial Pursuit: Dice decide how far you move round the board while you collect pie wedges. Two Canadians invented it in 1979 after a Scrabble game.
Board games that use dice.Ludo: Derived from India's Pachisi and patented in Britain in 1896. The name is Latin for I play.
Board games that use dice.Clue: Dice move you around the mansion. Birmingham's Anthony Pratt reportedly devised it during wartime air raids, patenting it in 1947 as Cluedo.
Board games that use dice.Parcheesi: The American trademark for India's Pachisi, sold since 1867. Cowrie shells were the original dice in the old Indian game.
Board games that use dice.Pictionary: A die moves teams round the board while one player sketches the clue. Seattle waiter Rob Angel invented it in 1985.
Board games that use dice.Snakes and Ladders: Based on India's Moksha Patam, where ladders stood for virtues and snakes for vices, so landing on a snake meant a moral lapse.
Board games that use dice.Game of Life: It uses a spinner, not dice, to move you through careers, marriage and houses.
Board games that use dice.Candy Land: Drawn cards decide your move, with no dice. Eleanor Abbott created it in 1948 while recovering from polio.
Board games that use dice.Sorry!: You draw cards instead of rolling dice. It descends from Pachisi, and sending a rival back to start earns the apology.
Board games that use dice.Chess: No dice at all: pure strategy. The number of possible games dwarfs the atoms in the observable universe.
Board games that use dice.Checkers: No luck involved. A team led by Jonathan Schaeffer proved in 2007 that perfect play always ends in a draw.
Board games that use dice.Go: No dice and no chance. It's over 2,500 years old, with far more possible positions than atoms in the universe.
Board games that use dice.Scrabble: Chance enters by drawing tiles from a bag, but dice play no part. Alfred Butts devised it during the Great Depression.
Board games that use dice.Stratego: Hidden ranked pieces, no dice: bluff and memory decide battles. It grew from the French game L'Attaque.
Board games that use dice.Connect Four: Players drop discs to line up four, with no dice or luck. A solver showed in 1988 that the first player can always win.
Board games that use dice.Othello: Disc-flipping with no luck involved. Modern Othello was devised in Japan in the 1970s from the older game Reversi.
Board games that use dice.Ticket to Ride: Cards, not dice, drive the rail-building. It won the 2004 Spiel des Jahres and spawned a large family of sequels.
Board games that use dice.Battleship: Players guess grid coordinates, no dice. It began as a pencil-and-paper game before Milton Bradley's 1967 plastic version.
Board games that use dice.Guess Who: Yes-or-no questions narrow down the faces. There are no dice, only deduction, which makes it a trap here.
Board games that use dice.Operation: A skill game with tweezers and a buzzer, so no dice. It came from a college project by John Spinello in the mid-1960s.

Words meaning a tied result.Draw: In chess a draw can be agreed by both players, and in football it earns each side a point.
Words meaning a tied result.Tie: In cricket a tie, level scores with all out, is far rarer than a draw. There have only been two in Test history.
Words meaning a tied result.Deadlock: The word began with a lock lacking a spring latch and spread to any standoff where neither side gives way.
Words meaning a tied result.Stalemate: In chess it happens when the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, and counts as a draw.
Words meaning a tied result.All square: Used in match play when neither player leads on holes. A golf phrase for level.
Words meaning a tied result.Dead heat: Used when two contestants cross the line together. In horse racing, bettors may be paid on shares of a tied result.
Words meaning a tied result.Push: In blackjack and betting a push is a tie where your stake is simply returned, so no one wins.
Words meaning a tied result.Level: British commentators say the scores are level, and in golf match play it can also mean all square.
Words meaning a tied result.Even: In golf, even par means your total equals par. It's a tie with the course, not an opponent.
Words meaning a tied result.Deuce: Tennis's 40-40, from French a deux de jeu, meaning two points needed. It is a tie you must break by two.
Words meaning a tied result.Shutout: The opposite of a tie, since the opponent scores zero and one side wins clearly.
Words meaning a tied result.Blowout: A lopsided result where one side crushes the other, the opposite of level.
Words meaning a tied result.Walkover: A win awarded when the opponent doesn't show up. No tie in sight.
Words meaning a tied result.Upset: When an underdog wins, which is a decisive result, not a tie.
Words meaning a tied result.Comeback: Ends with a winner. In 1993 Buffalo beat Houston 41-38 in overtime after trailing 35-3.
Words meaning a tied result.Whitewash: A clean sweep of a series, like 5-0 in cricket, so someone clearly wins.
Words meaning a tied result.Hat trick: Three goals by one player. The term comes from cricket, where taking three wickets in a row earned a hat.
Words meaning a tied result.Clean sheet: A team conceding no goals. It can still be a 0-0 draw, but the term itself isn't a tie.
Words meaning a tied result.Sudden death: A tiebreaker, not a tie. The first side to score in extra time wins immediately.
Words meaning a tied result.Love: Zero in tennis. It may come from French l'oeuf, an egg, though that theory is unproven.
Words meaning a tied result.Nil: British scoring word for zero. Nil-nil is a draw, but nil itself means zero.
Words meaning a tied result.Bye: A player advances without playing, and in cricket it's an extra run.
Words meaning a tied result.Forfeit: A loss by not playing, which gives someone else the win.
Words meaning a tied result.Rout: A crushing defeat, such as a 50-point blowout. It's the opposite of a tied result, since one side clearly wins.

Major esports titles.League of Legends: Riot's 2009 MOBA draws huge audiences; its World Championship finals have filled stadiums and drawn millions of viewers online.
Major esports titles.Dota 2: Valve's Dota 2 hosts The International, whose prize pool, boosted by fan purchases, passed $40 million in 2021.
Major esports titles.Counter-Strike: Born as a Half-Life mod in 1999, Counter-Strike became a pillar of competitive shooters, with major tournaments for decades.
Major esports titles.Valorant: Riot's tactical shooter launched in 2020, mixing gunplay with agent abilities, and quickly built a global esports circuit.
Major esports titles.Overwatch: Blizzard's 2016 hero shooter spawned the Overwatch League, with city-based teams like pro sports franchises.
Major esports titles.Rocket League: Soccer with rocket-powered cars, a hit that began as a free game in 2015 and grew into a major esport.
Major esports titles.StarCraft: StarCraft made esports a national obsession in South Korea, where pro gamers became celebrities and had TV channels.
Major esports titles.Fortnite: The 2019 Fortnite World Cup awarded $3 million to a 16-year-old solo winner, Kyle 'Bugha' Giersdorf.
Major esports titles.Call of Duty: Call of Duty has a pro league with city-based franchises, and its yearly releases are among the best-selling.
Major esports titles.Hearthstone: Blizzard's digital card game from 2014 has world championships, and it's among the top card esports.
Major esports titles.Apex Legends: A free battle royale from 2019 with squads of heroes, by Respawn, and it has a pro circuit called ALGS.
Major esports titles.Rainbow Six: Rainbow Six Siege is a tactical shooter focused on teamwork and destruction, a stalwart of esports.
Major esports titles.Animal Crossing: Animal Crossing is a relaxing life sim, which exploded in popularity in 2020, but it has no competitive scene.
Major esports titles.Stardew Valley: Stardew Valley is a farming sim made largely by one developer, Eric Barone, and it has no esports scene.
Major esports titles.The Sims: The Sims is a life simulation that has sold huge numbers worldwide, but it's not a competitive esport.
Major esports titles.Candy Crush: Candy Crush is a casual match-three mobile hit, not a major esports title.
Major esports titles.Angry Birds: Angry Birds launched in 2009 and was a casual mobile hit, not a competitive esport.
Major esports titles.Wii Fit: Wii Fit is a fitness game with the balance board, and not an esport.
Major esports titles.Nintendogs: Nintendogs is a virtual pet game for DS, and not competitive.
Major esports titles.Myst: Myst is a 1993 puzzle adventure that sold millions on CD-ROM, but it's single-player.
Major esports titles.Flappy Bird: Flappy Bird, from 2013, was withdrawn by its developer at its peak. It's not an esport.
Major esports titles.Farmville: FarmVille was a Facebook game of the late 2000s, at one point with tens of millions of daily players, but no esports.
Major esports titles.Journey: Journey is a 2012 artistic adventure game with anonymous co-op, not a competitive esport.
Major esports titles.Portal: Portal is a single-player puzzle game, famous for the line 'the cake is a lie'. It isn't a major esport.

Pet supplies.Leash: Retractable leashes can reach 8 meters, but vets warn the thin cord can cause burns and snaps, so many trainers prefer a fixed lead.
Pet supplies.Litter box: Cats are instinctive diggers who bury waste, and clumping clay litter was invented in 1947 by Ed Lowe, who sold it as 'Kitty Litter'.
Pet supplies.Food bowl: Flat, wide bowls suit flat-faced breeds and cats, and some cats dislike bowls that press on their whiskers, called whisker fatigue.
Pet supplies.Scratching post: Cats scratch to shed old claw sheaths, stretch muscles and leave scent from glands in their paws, not just to ruin furniture.
Pet supplies.Dog bed: Dogs sleep up to 12 to 14 hours a day, and many curl in a ring, an instinct that comes from wild ancestors who kept warm in dens.
Pet supplies.Birdcage: Covering a birdcage at night works because many parrots need 10 to 12 hours of dark, quiet sleep.
Pet supplies.Fish tank: Goldfish can live 10 years or more in good care, far beyond the fabled short life of a fish in a tiny bowl.
Pet supplies.Hamster wheel: Wild hamsters can run several kilometers each night, which is why a hamster needs a big, solid-surfaced wheel.
Pet supplies.Pet carrier: Leaving the carrier out with a blanket and treats helps a cat see it as a den, not a sign of a vet visit.
Pet supplies.Chew toy: Puppies chew when teething at about three to six months, and a frozen chew toy can ease sore gums.
Pet supplies.Flea comb: Fine-toothed combs trap fleas and flea dirt, and a damp white tissue turning red-brown shows the dirt is dried blood.
Pet supplies.Catnip: About half of cats react to catnip, an inherited trait, and the compound nepetalactone mimics a pheromone for a harmless high.
Pet supplies.Crib: A trap: a crib is baby furniture, and the word 'crib' for a baby's bed originally meant a manger for animal fodder.
Pet supplies.High chair: These are for human toddlers, so not a pet item, and the first high chairs were made for babies of the 1800s.
Pet supplies.Pacifier: Pacifiers soothe babies, not pets, and similar objects have been found in ancient graves, a very old human invention.
Pet supplies.Sippy cup: Sippy cups were patented in the 1950s for young kids, and a puppy would not know what to do with one.
Pet supplies.Diaper bag: A diaper bag is for babies, and carries wipes, a change mat and spare clothes rather than a dog's treats.
Pet supplies.Baby monitor: Baby monitors were inspired by the Lindbergh kidnapping in 1932, when Zenith made an early 'radio nurse' for the case.
Pet supplies.Bib: Bibs catch drool and spills for babies, and the word probably comes from 'bibber', someone who drinks a lot.
Pet supplies.Rattle: Rattles are among the oldest toys, and babies seem to respond to the noise from just a few months old.
Pet supplies.Changing table: The changing table is for human babies, and the table was first marketed in the 1950s when diaper pins ruled.
Pet supplies.Onesie: The baby bodysuit snaps at the crotch, a design that keeps the shirt from riding up, and it comes from the 1930s-50s.
Pet supplies.Teething ring: Teething rings are chilled, not frozen, for infants whose teeth begin arriving around six months.
Pet supplies.Potty chair: A potty chair is for toilet-training toddlers, whereas a pet's needs are handled by the litter box or the yard.

Things you usually do before bed.Brush your teeth: Dentists advise brushing before bed because saliva flow drops during sleep, which lets bacteria work on teeth for hours.
Things you usually do before bed.Set an alarm: Surveys find many adults rely on a phone alarm, and the first mechanical alarm clock was built in 1787 by an American, Levi Hutchins, to wake at 4 a.m.
Things you usually do before bed.Put on pajamas: The word comes from the Hindi 'pajama', loose trousers worn by Indians, and British colonials brought the style home.
Things you usually do before bed.Turn off the lights: Darkness lets the body release melatonin, and bright blue light from screens can delay that.
Things you usually do before bed.Lock the door: A final lock check is a bedtime habit worldwide, and many people also test the handle twice.
Things you usually do before bed.Wash your face: Washing off makeup and grime at night helps skin recover, as it repairs itself overnight.
