Things you usually do before bed.Charge your phone: Overnight charging is common, and modern phones stop charging at full, so it does little harm.
Things you usually do before bed.Draw the curtains: Blackout curtains can block street light, and a darker room helps with deeper sleep.
Things you usually do before bed.Fluff your pillow: Down pillows regain loft when shaken, and the habit goes back centuries.
Things you usually do before bed.Say goodnight: Many cultures have a bedtime ritual, and a calm routine helps children fall asleep faster.
Things you usually do before bed.Eat breakfast: Breakfast is a morning meal, and the word means breaking the night's fast.
Things you usually do before bed.Make coffee: Coffee in the morning is a global habit, and caffeine takes about 30 to 60 minutes to peak in your blood.
Things you usually do before bed.Eat lunch: Lunch is midday, and the English word may come from 'luncheon', a thick piece of food.
Things you usually do before bed.Open the curtains: Morning light helps reset the body clock, and that is why people open curtains when they wake.
Things you usually do before bed.Commute to work: The average commute in the US is about 27 minutes each way, a daytime activity.
Things you usually do before bed.Make the bed: Making the bed is a morning chore, and a naval admiral famously said it can start your day with a win.
Things you usually do before bed.Hit snooze: A snooze button gives a short nap of about nine minutes on many alarms, a quirk from 1950s clock design.
Things you usually do before bed.Turn off the alarm: Switching off the alarm is how a morning begins, whereas bedtime is when you set it.
Things you usually do before bed.Walk to school: It is a morning commute for children, so it comes after waking up.
Things you usually do before bed.Put on shoes: Shoes are for heading out, so you take them off when you get in for the night.
Things you usually do before bed.Watch the sunrise: A sunrise is an early-morning event, long after bedtime.
Things you usually do before bed.Do the school run: The school run is the morning crush of parents driving kids in, which is no bedtime task.
Things you usually do before bed.Take a lunch break: Lunch comes around noon, hours before bed.
Things you usually do before bed.Leave for work: Leaving for work is morning, and so ends the sleep side of the day.

Things a dog would happily fetch.Stick: Dogs love sticks, but splintered ones can injure the mouth, so vets often prefer a rubber alternative.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Tennis ball: Tennis balls are fuzzy, which can wear down teeth like sandpaper, so some vets suggest rubber balls for hard chewers.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Frisbee: Disc dogs date to 1974, when a whippet named Ashley interrupted a baseball game to catch a Frisbee on live TV.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Newspaper: The dog bringing the newspaper is real, since retrievers were bred to carry things back gently.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Slipper: Fetching slippers is a classic cliche, probably helped along by a dog's fondness for the scent of your worn shoes.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Rubber ball: A rubber ball bounces unpredictably, which triggers a dog's chase instinct.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Squeaky toy: The squeak mimics a prey animal's cry, which is why many dogs go wild for it.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Rope toy: Rope toys double as dental floss, and tug-of-war with a dog is fine in moderation.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Chew bone: Dogs love chewing bones, but cooked bones are dangerous, and a rubber or nylon chew is safer.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Bowling ball: A bowling ball weighs 3 to 7 kilos, far too heavy for a dog to carry, and could injure its teeth.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Car: No dog can fetch a car, though in 2012 shelter dogs in New Zealand were trained to drive a modified one.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Sofa: A sofa is too heavy and bulky for a dog to carry, but plenty of dogs claim one as their own.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Anchor: Anchors weigh from a few kilos to many tonnes, far beyond any dog's carrying power.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Refrigerator: A fridge is far heavier than any dog, even a 50-kilo Newfoundland, a breed strong enough to rescue swimmers.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Piano: Pianos weigh hundreds of kilos, far beyond even the strongest dog.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Bathtub: A bathtub is unwieldy, and dogs more often hate being in one than want to carry it.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Boulder: Boulders weigh tonnes, and dogs that carry rocks can wear their teeth down badly.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Bus: A bus is more than a thousand times heavier than a large dog.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Tractor: Tractors weigh several tonnes, and no dog could move one, let alone bring it back.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Wardrobe: A wardrobe is bulky and heavy, so no dog can fetch it, though many dogs enjoy hiding inside.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Washing machine: Washing machines weigh around 70 kilos, more than most dogs can fetch, though dogs often steal socks from them.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Canoe: Dogs love riding in canoes, but fetching one is another story; a canoe is many times longer than a dog.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Treadmill: Dogs can walk on treadmills for exercise, but no dog can fetch one.
Things a dog would happily fetch.Lawnmower: Dogs often bark at lawnmowers, and fetching one is impossible for any dog.

Animals that aren't what their name says.Koala bear: A koala is a marsupial, not a bear, and it sleeps up to 20 hours a day because its eucalyptus diet gives little energy.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Jellyfish: A jellyfish is not a fish; it has no bones or brain, and it is more closely related to corals and anemones.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Starfish: Starfish are not fish but echinoderms, relatives of sea urchins, which is why scientists prefer the name sea star.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Guinea pig: A guinea pig is neither from Guinea nor a pig; it is a rodent from the Andes, where people have kept them as food for thousands of years.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Seahorse: A seahorse is a fish, though it does not swim like one, and it is the male who carries the eggs and gives birth.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Flying fox: A flying fox is a big fruit bat, not a fox, and the largest species have wingspans of about 1.5 meters.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Sea lion: A sea lion is a seal-like mammal with external ear flaps, not a lion, and it can walk on land using its flippers.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Prairie dog: A prairie dog is a rodent, not a dog, with the name from its bark-like warning calls, which can even describe a predator's color.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Silverfish: A silverfish is a wingless insect, not a fish, that has existed for hundreds of millions of years.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Catfish: A catfish gets its name from whisker-like barbels, and these whiskers carry taste buds, so it tastes with its entire body.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Horned toad: A horned toad is a lizard, not a toad, and it can squirt blood from its eyes to scare off predators.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Sea cucumber: A sea cucumber is an animal, not a vegetable, and some can expel their guts to distract a predator, then regrow them.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Polar bear: A polar bear is really a bear, and its skin is black under translucent fur, helping absorb the sun's heat.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Goldfish: A goldfish is a fish and gold-colored, and with proper care one can live over 20 years, with a memory of months, not seconds.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Grizzly bear: A grizzly is a brown bear, and its name refers to the grizzled silver-tipped fur, not to a grisly nature.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Brown bear: The brown bear is the most widespread bear in the world, and its name matches its usual coat color.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Blue whale: A blue whale is a whale, and it really looks blue-gray under water, which makes the name accurate.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Black bear: A black bear is a bear, but it can be cinnamon, blond, or even white, which only half fits its name.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Sea turtle: A sea turtle is a real turtle that lives in the sea, and it comes ashore only to lay eggs on the beach it hatched on.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Barn owl: A barn owl is really an owl that often nests in barns, and its heart-shaped face helps it locate prey by sound.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Honeybee: A honeybee is a real bee that makes honey, and a worker makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her life.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Tree frog: A tree frog is a frog that does live in trees, and its sticky toe pads let it climb on glass.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Box turtle: A box turtle is a real turtle that can shut its shell like a box, thanks to a hinge on its belly.
Animals that aren't what their name says.Snowy owl: A snowy owl is really an owl and really snowy, living in the Arctic tundra with its white feathers.

Magic words.Abracadabra: Abracadabra may come from Aramaic, 'I create as I speak', and a Roman physician once prescribed it written in a triangle to cure fever.
Magic words.Hocus pocus: Hocus pocus may be a mock-Latin phrase used by 1600s conjurers; some say it mocks the Catholic Mass words 'hoc est corpus'.
Magic words.Alakazam: Alakazam is a stage-magic exclamation, and the name was borrowed for a Pokemon who shares the magic-user image.
Magic words.Open sesame: Open sesame is the command in Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves that opens the robbers' cave; the tale was added to The Arabian Nights by Antoine Galland.
Magic words.Presto: Presto is Italian for quick, and magicians say it as the moment of change; in music it means a very fast tempo.
Magic words.Shazam: Shazam is the word that turns Billy Batson into the superhero Captain Marvel, an acronym of six mythic figures' names.
Magic words.Bibbidi-bobbidi-boo: Bibbidi-bobbidi-boo is the fairy godmother's spell in Disney's Cinderella (1950), which was nominated for an Oscar.
Magic words.Sim sala bim: Sim sala bim is a magician's phrase made famous by Danish magician Dante in the 20th century.
Magic words.Expelliarmus: Expelliarmus is the disarming spell in Harry Potter, from Latin 'expellere' meaning to drive out and 'arma', weapons.
Magic words.Wingardium Leviosa: Wingardium Leviosa is the levitation charm in Harry Potter, with the emphasis on 'Levi-O-sa', not 'Levio-sa'.
Magic words.Please: Please is the original magic word, as parents say, and it's a fine trick: asking politely does open doors.
Magic words.Bingo: A trap: bingo is shouted to claim a win at a game, and while it sounds magical, it's no spell.
Magic words.Yahtzee: Yahtzee is a dice game's name and what you shout for five of a kind; it's a trademark, not a spell.
Magic words.Cheese: Cheese is said to make people smile for photos, which might feel like magic, but it isn't a spell.
Magic words.Gesundheit: Gesundheit is German for 'health', said after a sneeze; the habit may come from fear of a lost soul.
Magic words.Eureka: Eureka is Greek for 'I have found it', supposedly shouted by Archimedes in his bath; it's a discovery word, not a spell.
Magic words.Timber: Timber is a lumberjack's warning that a tree is falling, not a magic word.
Magic words.Checkmate: Checkmate comes from Persian 'shah mat', meaning the king is helpless or 'the king is stumped', and it isn't a spell.
Magic words.Fore: Fore is the golfer's warning for those ahead; it's likely short for 'beware before' and doesn't cast spells.
Magic words.Touchdown: Touchdown is a football score worth six points, and no spell, even though it feels magical for fans.
Magic words.Gotcha: Gotcha is a casual 'I got you', and you'd say it after a prank, not as a spell.
Magic words.Bless you: Bless you is said after a sneeze, a custom that may come from old fears about the soul escaping.
Magic words.Jackpot: Jackpot is a big win, from poker where the pot built up until a pair of jacks or better; it's no spell.
Magic words.Bazinga: Bazinga is Sheldon's catchphrase in The Big Bang Theory, and it signals a joke, not a spell.

Microsoft products.Word: Microsoft Word first came out in 1983, and its .doc and .docx files became the default for documents worldwide.
Microsoft products.Excel: Excel arrived on the Mac in 1985 before Windows, and its grid of cells has 1,048,576 rows in recent versions.
Microsoft products.PowerPoint: PowerPoint was created at Forethought and bought by Microsoft in 1987 for about 14 million dollars.
Microsoft products.Outlook: Outlook began as part of Office in 1997, and it's both the email and calendar app.
Microsoft products.OneNote: OneNote is a digital notebook, launched in 2003, that lets you write or draw anywhere on a page.
Microsoft products.Teams: Teams launched in 2017 and grew sharply in 2020 when remote work boomed during the pandemic.
Microsoft products.Xbox: Xbox launched in 2001 as Microsoft's console to compete with PlayStation, with Halo as its launch hit.
Microsoft products.Windows: Windows 1.0 appeared in 1985 as a graphical add-on to the text-based MS-DOS.
Microsoft products.Bing: Bing, launched in 2009, replaced Live Search and also powers some chatbot search features.
Microsoft products.Edge: Edge replaced Internet Explorer, and since 2020 it uses Chromium, the same engine behind Chrome.
Microsoft products.Visual Studio: Visual Studio is Microsoft's suite for writing code, and it first came out in 1997.
Microsoft products.LinkedIn: Microsoft bought LinkedIn in 2016 for about 26 billion dollars, its largest deal at the time.
Microsoft products.Photoshop: Photoshop belongs to Adobe, whereas Microsoft's own image editor is Paint, which has shipped with Windows since 1985.
Microsoft products.Keynote: Keynote is Apple's presentation app, built for Steve Jobs's talks, and it rivals PowerPoint.
Microsoft products.Gmail: Gmail is Google's email, launched on April 1, 2004, a date that made many people think it was a joke.
Microsoft products.Slack: Slack has belonged to Salesforce since 2021, and it competes with Microsoft's Teams.
Microsoft products.Zoom: Zoom is a separate company, and its popularity exploded in 2020, challenging Microsoft Teams.
Microsoft products.Chrome: Chrome is Google's browser, launched in 2008, and it's the world's most used browser.
Microsoft products.Safari: Safari is Apple's browser, first released for the Mac in 2003.
Microsoft products.Acrobat: Acrobat is Adobe's PDF software, while Microsoft Word offers its own save-as-PDF option.
Microsoft products.Firefox: Firefox is made by Mozilla, which grew from Netscape, once the main rival of Microsoft's Internet Explorer.
Microsoft products.Android: Android is Google's mobile operating system, and Microsoft's Windows Phone never managed to dent it.
Microsoft products.PlayStation: PlayStation is Sony's console, a rival to Xbox, first launched in 1994 in Japan.
Microsoft products.iPhone: The iPhone came out in 2007 from Apple, while Microsoft's phones used Windows Phone and never caught on.

Things a sushi chef uses.Bamboo mat: A makisu, the bamboo mat, rolls maki, and sushi chefs often wrap it in plastic to stop rice sticking.
Things a sushi chef uses.Sushi rice: Sushi rice is a short-grain variety seasoned with vinegar, and chefs say the rice matters as much as the fish.
Things a sushi chef uses.Nori: Nori is dried seaweed pressed into thin sheets, and the process was developed in Japan centuries ago.
Things a sushi chef uses.Wasabi: Real wasabi is a rare plant that is hard to grow, and most tubes of it actually contain dyed horseradish.
Things a sushi chef uses.Raw fish: The word sushi actually refers to the vinegared rice, not the fish, and raw fish is often frozen first to kill parasites.
Things a sushi chef uses.Rice vinegar: Vinegar gives sushi rice its tang, and the dish began as a way to preserve fish by fermenting it in rice.
Things a sushi chef uses.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is made by fermenting soybeans and wheat, and sushi chefs often brush it on the fish for you.
Things a sushi chef uses.Pickled ginger: Pickled ginger, called gari, is eaten between pieces to refresh your palate, not put on top of the sushi.
Things a sushi chef uses.Rice paddle: The rice paddle, or shamoji, is used to fold vinegar through hot rice without mashing it.
Things a sushi chef uses.Sashimi knife: A yanagiba is a long, slim sashimi knife that slices fish in one smooth pull for clean cuts.
Things a sushi chef uses.Sesame seeds: Sesame seeds coat inside-out rolls such as the California roll, which put the rice on the outside.
Things a sushi chef uses.Pizza peel: A pizza peel moves pies in and out of ovens, and it has no part in handling rice.
Things a sushi chef uses.Tortilla press: A tortilla press flattens masa; sushi is Japanese but tortillas are Mexican.
Things a sushi chef uses.Waffle iron: Waffle irons are a Belgian-style breakfast tool, and don't belong at a sushi counter.
Things a sushi chef uses.Mozzarella: Mozzarella is an Italian cheese, traditionally made from buffalo milk, with no place in traditional sushi.
Things a sushi chef uses.Pasta maker: A pasta maker rolls and cuts dough, an Italian tool, whereas sushi uses rice.
Things a sushi chef uses.Croissant: Croissants are buttery French pastry, and sushi uses no baking or dairy.
Things a sushi chef uses.Maple syrup: Maple syrup is boiled tree sap from Canada and the northeast US, and it takes about 40 litres of sap to make one litre.
Things a sushi chef uses.Corn tortillas: Corn tortillas come from Mexico's nixtamalised maize, and they're not rice-based.
Things a sushi chef uses.Bagels: Bagels are boiled and baked dough rings, with roots in the Jewish communities of Poland.
Things a sushi chef uses.Tomato sauce: Tomatoes came from the Americas and weren't in Europe until the 1500s, so tomato sauce is a late Italian classic.
Things a sushi chef uses.Cheddar: Cheddar takes its name from a village in Somerset, England, and isn't used in traditional sushi.
Things a sushi chef uses.Baguette: French law once set rules for the traditional baguette: only flour, water, salt and yeast.
Things a sushi chef uses.Gravy boat: A gravy boat serves sauce at roast dinners, not at a sushi counter.

Things a pizza chef uses.Pizza peel: A peel is a long paddle that slides pizza into hot ovens, with a wooden one for building and a metal one for turning.
Things a pizza chef uses.Pizza oven: Neapolitan ovens burn at around 450 degrees Celsius and bake a pizza in about 90 seconds.
Things a pizza chef uses.Pizza cutter: A rocker or wheel cutter slices through hot cheese without dragging the toppings away.
Things a pizza chef uses.Dough: Neapolitan dough is simple, just flour, water, salt and yeast, but it ferments for many hours for flavour.
Things a pizza chef uses.Mozzarella: Pizza Margherita is said to have been named for Queen Margherita in 1889, with white mozzarella standing in for the white of Italy's flag.
Things a pizza chef uses.Tomato sauce: Early pizzas often had no tomato, since tomatoes only reached Italy after arriving from the Americas.
Things a pizza chef uses.Basil: Basil's green stands for the green of Italy's flag on a Margherita.
Things a pizza chef uses.Olive oil: A drizzle of olive oil finishes a pizza, and Italy and Spain are among the top producers.
Things a pizza chef uses.Oregano: Oregano means 'joy of the mountain' in Greek, and it's a classic pizza herb.
Things a pizza chef uses.Pizza stone: A pizza stone absorbs heat and gives a crisp bottom, similar to the floor of a brick oven.
Things a pizza chef uses.Wok: A wok's curved bottom focuses heat for stir-frying, an Asian technique rather than a pizza chef's.
Things a pizza chef uses.Sushi mat: A sushi mat rolls maki, so it's a sushi chef's tool and not a pizza chef's.
Things a pizza chef uses.Tortilla press: A tortilla press is for Mexican flatbreads, which are a bit like pizza but made from masa or flour dough.
Things a pizza chef uses.Waffle iron: Waffle irons press batter into a grid, which is a breakfast tool and not for pizza.
Things a pizza chef uses.Bamboo steamer: Bamboo steamers cook dumplings and buns, stacked in tiers over a pot.
Things a pizza chef uses.Chopsticks: Chopsticks pick up noodles and sushi, and they're not for pizza slices.
Things a pizza chef uses.Nori: Nori is dried seaweed used to wrap sushi, so it's not a pizza chef's ingredient.
Things a pizza chef uses.Wasabi: Wasabi is a pungent Japanese condiment for sushi, and it doesn't go on pizza.
Things a pizza chef uses.Rice cooker: A rice cooker steams rice with an automatic cut-off, which a pizza kitchen doesn't need.
Things a pizza chef uses.Fondue fork: A fondue fork dips bread into melted cheese, and while Swiss fondue and pizza both celebrate melted cheese, it's not a pizza tool.
Things a pizza chef uses.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is a salty, fermented seasoning from Asia, and it's not a pizza ingredient.
Things a pizza chef uses.Tandoor: A tandoor is a clay oven used in India that bakes naan, a flatbread cousin to pizza, but it's not a pizza oven.
Things a pizza chef uses.Egg poacher: An egg poacher cooks eggs gently in water, and a pizza chef would just bake the egg on top in the oven.
Things a pizza chef uses.Dim sum basket: A dim sum basket steams dumplings in Chinese teahouses, which has nothing to do with pizza.

Things a land surveyor uses.Theodolite: A telescope mounted to measure horizontal and vertical angles; the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India used huge ones.
Things a land surveyor uses.Total station: Combines a theodolite with a laser distance meter, so one instrument gives angle and distance to within millimetres.
Things a land surveyor uses.Tripod: A three-legged stand holds instruments steady and level on uneven ground, because three legs always touch the ground.
Things a land surveyor uses.Leveling rod: A tall graduated staff held upright over a point; the surveyor reads the height through the level's telescope.
Things a land surveyor uses.Measuring wheel: A wheel of known circumference clicks a counter as it rolls, giving distance on the ground quickly.
Things a land surveyor uses.GPS receiver: Survey-grade GPS with corrections can fix positions to within centimetres, far better than a phone's several metres.
Things a land surveyor uses.Survey prism: A retroreflector bounces the total station's beam straight back so the instrument can calculate distance.
Things a land surveyor uses.Plumb bob: A weight on a string that hangs straight down, a tool builders used to check verticals thousands of years ago.
Things a land surveyor uses.Marking paint: Spray paint colour codes mark buried utilities in the US; red, for example, means electric.
Things a land surveyor uses.Field book: Surveyors' notes are legal records, kept in permanent ink, with errors crossed out rather than erased.
Things a land surveyor uses.Survey stakes: Wooden stakes with flagging mark points on the ground; George Washington worked as a surveyor in his teens.
Things a land surveyor uses.Stethoscope: A doctor's listening tool, no use for measuring land.
Things a land surveyor uses.Whisk: A kitchen tool; a flat, level result is what both cooks and surveyors fuss over.
Things a land surveyor uses.Saddle: A horse's seat; early American surveyors did ride, but modern kit goes by truck.
Things a land surveyor uses.Easel: A painter's frame; a surveyor's plot is drawn on a plan table, not an easel.
Things a land surveyor uses.Loom: A weaving machine; the old Gunter's chain, 66 feet of links, was the surveyor's real long tool.
Things a land surveyor uses.Fishing rod: An extended rod may resemble a leveling rod, but it catches fish, not heights.
Things a land surveyor uses.Piping bag: A baker's tool for icing; surveyors do locate buried pipes before digging starts.
Things a land surveyor uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet; boundary disputes do end up before judges after surveyors' work.
Things a land surveyor uses.Baton: A conductor's stick; surveyors' range poles look similar but are painted red and white for visibility.
Things a land surveyor uses.Kiln: A potter's furnace; survey markers are bronze or concrete, not fired clay.
Things a land surveyor uses.Plunger: A plumber's helper; surveyors mark sewer lines but never unclog them.
Things a land surveyor uses.Tuning fork: Vibrates at a fixed pitch; surveyors rely on lasers and light, not sound.
Things a land surveyor uses.Paint roller: A decorator's tool; surveyors use spray cans to mark ground points.

1980s home computers.Commodore 64: Launched in 1982, it is often cited as the best-selling single computer model ever, with estimates of 12 to 17 million units.
1980s home computers.ZX Spectrum: Sinclair's rubber-keyed 1982 micro made Britain a nation of bedroom coders and launched many game studios.
1980s home computers.Atari ST: Its built-in MIDI ports made it a favorite of musicians, and it stayed a studio staple long after the 1980s.
1980s home computers.Amiga: Its 1985 launch brought advanced graphics and sound years ahead of rivals, and a cult following that persists.
1980s home computers.BBC Micro: Built by Acorn for a BBC literacy project, it put computers in British schools; Acorn's later ARM chip now powers most phones.
1980s home computers.Amstrad CPC: Amstrad's 1984 line came bundled with its own monitor, which kept it cheap and made it a hit in Europe.
1980s home computers.MSX: A 1983 standard backed by Microsoft Japan that let makers build compatible machines; Metal Gear began life on MSX2.
1980s home computers.Macintosh: The 1984 original, introduced with a famous Super Bowl ad, popularized the mouse and graphical desktop for the public.
1980s home computers.IBM PC: IBM's 1981 design used off-the-shelf parts, which let clone makers copy it and made the PC platform the industry standard.
1980s home computers.VIC-20: In 1982 it became the first computer to sell a million units, with William Shatner starring in its TV ads.
1980s home computers.Tandy 1000: Radio Shack's 1984 PC compatible for homes had improved graphics and sound that many early DOS games supported by name.
1980s home computers.Acorn Electron: A cut-down, cheaper BBC Micro sold from 1983, famously short of stock in its first Christmas.
1980s home computers.iMac: Apple's colorful all-in-one launched in 1998, so it belongs to the 1990s, and revived the company.
1980s home computers.PlayStation: Sony's console arrived in 1994 in Japan. It began as a failed collaboration with Nintendo on a CD add-on.
1980s home computers.Game Boy: Nintendo's handheld came out in 1989 and was a console, not a home computer. Tetris bundled with it helped it sell.
1980s home computers.NES: Nintendo's console, released in Japan as the Famicom in 1983, was a game system, not a computer.
1980s home computers.Sega Genesis: Sega's 16-bit console debuted in 1988 in Japan as Mega Drive; a game machine, not a computer.
1980s home computers.iPad: Released in 2010, it's decades too late for this list. Apple sold over 300 million by the late 2010s.
1980s home computers.ThinkPad: IBM launched it in 1992, and its red TrackPoint nub became an icon; this is too late for the 1980s.
1980s home computers.Chromebook: Google's web-focused laptops arrived in 2011, well after the 1980s home computer era.
1980s home computers.Raspberry Pi: This credit-card computer from 2012 was inspired partly by the BBC Micro, but it is much younger.
1980s home computers.Surface: Microsoft's own-brand tablets began in 2012, far past the 1980s.
1980s home computers.MacBook: Apple introduced the name in 2006, when it replaced the PowerBook and iBook lines.
1980s home computers.Nintendo 64: Launched in 1996 in Japan, it's a console, not a 1980s home computer.

Tech and gaming conventions.CES: Held every January in Las Vegas, the Consumer Electronics Show is where companies preview gadgets, from TVs to robots.
Tech and gaming conventions.WWDC: Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference, usually in June, is where new versions of iOS and macOS are first shown.
Tech and gaming conventions.Google I/O: Google's annual developer conference; the name nods to input/output and the phrase Innovation in the Open.
Tech and gaming conventions.E3: Once gaming's biggest annual show in Los Angeles, it was cancelled for good in 2023 after years of decline.
Tech and gaming conventions.Gamescom: Held in Cologne, Germany, since 2009, it is Europe's biggest games event and draws hundreds of thousands of visitors.
Tech and gaming conventions.Web Summit: This huge tech conference began in Dublin in 2010 and moved to Lisbon in 2016.
Tech and gaming conventions.DEF CON: A Las Vegas hacker gathering, held since 1993, famous for contests like capture the flag and badges that act as puzzles.
Tech and gaming conventions.MWC: Mobile World Congress takes place in Barcelona each year and is the largest event for the mobile industry.
Tech and gaming conventions.PAX: Penny Arcade's Expo began in Seattle in 2004 and spawned editions in Boston, Melbourne and elsewhere.
Tech and gaming conventions.Dreamforce: Salesforce's yearly conference takes over downtown San Francisco and draws tens of thousands of attendees.
Tech and gaming conventions.Black Hat: This security conference in Las Vegas runs just before DEF CON, and is more corporate and expensive.
Tech and gaming conventions.Computex: Taipei's yearly computer trade show is where chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD often reveal new hardware.
Tech and gaming conventions.Comic-Con: San Diego's giant pop-culture convention covers comics, film and TV panels more than tech, which is why it feels close but isn't.
Tech and gaming conventions.Coachella: A California music and arts festival, held in the desert every April, not a tech convention.
Tech and gaming conventions.Glastonbury: A huge UK music festival, famous for mud and a famous Pyramid Stage, not a tech event.
Tech and gaming conventions.Burning Man: An annual desert gathering in Nevada that ends with burning a giant wooden effigy; an arts event, not a tech expo.
Tech and gaming conventions.Woodstock: The 1969 New York music festival that drew roughly 400,000 people; nothing to do with tech conventions.
Tech and gaming conventions.Super Bowl: It is America's championship football game, and famous for its pricey ads, though some tech firms have debuted there.
Tech and gaming conventions.Met Gala: A fashion fundraiser for New York's Costume Institute, held each May with a themed red carpet.
Tech and gaming conventions.Wimbledon: The oldest tennis tournament in the world, played on grass in London since 1877.
Tech and gaming conventions.Oscars: Film's top awards, handed out as gold statuettes officially named the Academy Award of Merit.
Tech and gaming conventions.Grammys: Music's biggest awards night, named for the gramophone trophy.
Tech and gaming conventions.Sundance: A Utah film festival founded by Robert Redford's institute, famous for launching indie films.
Tech and gaming conventions.Lollapalooza: A Chicago music festival started in 1991 as a touring farewell for Jane's Addiction.

Source code file extensions..py: Python scripts. Guido van Rossum named the language after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake.
Source code file extensions..js: JavaScript files. Brendan Eich created the first version of the language in about ten days in 1995, at Netscape.
Source code file extensions..java: Java source files that compile into bytecode, so the same program can run on any machine with a Java Virtual Machine.
Source code file extensions..c: C source files. Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs in the early 1970s, and it remains the base of many operating systems.
Source code file extensions..cpp: C++ source. Bjarne Stroustrup began it as C with Classes in 1979, and it's used in games and browsers.
Source code file extensions..rb: Ruby scripts. Yukihiro Matsumoto designed the language in Japan to be pleasant to read and write, and it powers Rails.
Source code file extensions..go: Source files in Google's Go language, designed to compile quickly into standalone programs.
Source code file extensions..rs: Rust source files. The language began as a personal project and aims at speed with memory safety, and is loved by developers.
Source code file extensions..swift: Swift is Apple's language for iPhone and Mac apps, introduced at WWDC in 2014 to succeed Objective-C.
Source code file extensions..php: PHP scripts power a huge share of websites, including WordPress, and the language began as simple tools in 1994.
Source code file extensions..ts: TypeScript source, though .ts also marks MPEG transport stream video files, an easy collision that has confused many tools.
Source code file extensions..kt: Kotlin source files. JetBrains made the language, and Google named it a preferred language for Android development in 2019.
Source code file extensions..jpg: A JPEG photo is image data, so it can't be run or compiled; the letters jpg stand for a photographic experts group.
Source code file extensions..mp3: MP3 holds compressed audio, which a computer plays rather than runs; a human can't read its contents as code.
Source code file extensions..pdf: A PDF is a fixed-layout document, not code, despite being able to embed scripts in some cases.
Source code file extensions..docx: A Word document, secretly a zip of XML files, which makes it a data container and not a source file.
Source code file extensions..exe: Executables are the compiled result of source code, so they are the product, not the source.
Source code file extensions..zip: A zip is a compressed bundle that might contain source code but isn't itself code.
Source code file extensions..png: PNG is a lossless image format designed as a patent-free alternative to GIF, so it's pictures, not code.
Source code file extensions..wav: WAV stores raw, uncompressed audio, which makes for large files, and is data, not code.
Source code file extensions..gif: A GIF is a 1987 image format famous for short looping animations, so it holds pixels, not source.
Source code file extensions..mov: A MOV is Apple's QuickTime video container, so it holds video and audio, not code.
Source code file extensions..xls: An Excel spreadsheet file in the old binary format, which can hold macros, but it isn't source code.
Source code file extensions..ppt: A PowerPoint presentation in the old binary format, so slides, not source code.

Things with a lens.Camera: Most cameras use several glass lens elements, and a good lens often matters more to image quality than the sensor.
Things with a lens.Webcam: Most laptops carry one, and a tiny sliding cover over the lens has become a popular privacy fix.
Things with a lens.Projector: A projector's lens focuses light from a bright lamp or laser onto a distant screen, enlarging the picture.
Things with a lens.Telescope: Galileo's 1609 versions used simple lenses, and he used them to spot the moons of Jupiter.
Things with a lens.Microscope: Anton van Leeuwenhoek's tiny single-lens versions let him see bacteria in the 1600s.
Things with a lens.Binoculars: Binoculars use two lens systems with prisms, which flip the image upright and fold the long light path to shorten the body.
Things with a lens.Eyeglasses: The first wearable ones date to 13th-century Italy, and the inventor remains unknown.
Things with a lens.Magnifying glass: It is arguably the simplest lens a person can hold; a single curved piece of glass makes things look bigger.
Things with a lens.GoPro: Its tiny wide-angle lens lets the action camera capture a very wide scene, and it was founded by Nick Woodman.
Things with a lens.Lighthouse: A Fresnel lens, a ring-shaped glass design from the 1820s, lets a lighthouse beam shine for many miles.
Things with a lens.VR headset: Lenses between your eyes and the screen make a small display fill your vision and look far away.
Things with a lens.Peephole: A peephole contains a wide fisheye lens so someone inside can see a broad scene outside a door.
Things with a lens.Speaker: Inside is a cone and magnet, no lens, which works by moving air.
Things with a lens.Keyboard: No lens here: a keyboard's keys are plain switches, though some are backlit by LEDs.
Things with a lens.Toaster: A toaster heats wire elements; it has no lens at all.
Things with a lens.Radio: Radios catch invisible waves with an antenna, with no lens involved.
Things with a lens.Router: A router directs data packets and has no lens, though its antennas may look like they could.
Things with a lens.Calculator: Its display is typically a simple liquid-crystal panel, with no lens.
Things with a lens.Thermostat: A thermostat senses temperature with a bimetal strip or electronic sensor, not a lens.
Things with a lens.Headphones: Headphones turn electrical signals into sound with a driver and have no lens.
Things with a lens.Microwave: A microwave's glass window is covered by a metal mesh, but there is no lens.
Things with a lens.Joystick: A joystick tracks the movement of a lever; no lens is involved, though optical versions exist in some.
Things with a lens.Hairdryer: A hairdryer pushes air over a heating element and has no lens.
Things with a lens.Stapler: Stapler bends metal through paper, with no lens in sight.

Famous paintings (not sculptures).Mona Lisa: The Louvre's star, stolen in 1911 by a museum worker; the theft and press coverage made it world-famous.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Starry Night: Van Gogh painted it in 1889 from his asylum room in Saint-Rémy; the village was partly invented.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Scream: Munch made several versions; one was stolen from an Oslo museum in 2004, and another sold for about $120 million in 2012.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Guernica: Picasso's black-and-white protest of the 1937 bombing of a Basque town; a tapestry copy at the UN was covered during 2003 Iraq announcements.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).American Gothic: Grant Wood's 1930 farm couple are really a dentist and the artist's sister, not husband and wife.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Nighthawks: Hopper's 1942 late-night diner scene in Chicago, now in the Art Institute of Chicago.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Night Watch: Rembrandt's 1642 militia portrait is actually a daytime scene; darkened varnish gave the false impression of night.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Las Meninas: Velázquez's 1656 court scene, in which the painter himself stands at an easel, with a mirror reflecting the king and queen.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Water Lilies: Monet's late series, painted in his garden at Giverny, fills oval rooms at the Orangerie in Paris.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Birth of Venus: Botticelli's Venus arrives on a scallop shell; it hangs in the Uffizi, Florence, and the goddess is shown in the Renaissance's idea of beauty.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Last Supper: Leonardo's wall painting in Milan; his experimental technique began to flake within decades of completion.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Whistler's Mother: Officially titled Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, Whistler's 1871 portrait of his mother hangs in Paris.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Christina's World: Andrew Wyeth's 1948 painting shows Christina Olson, who had a muscle disorder, crawling across a field in Maine.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).The Thinker: A bronze by Rodin; it began as a figure for The Gates of Hell, a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Venus de Milo: A marble statue found on the island of Milos in 1820, missing both arms; it is a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Discobolus: A Greek sculpture by Myron, known mostly through Roman copies; a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Winged Victory: A marble Hellenistic statue in the Louvre, a sculpture, shown on a ship's prow.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Manneken Pis: A famous small bronze fountain in Brussels, a boy relieving himself, with hundreds of costumes.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Statue of Liberty: A giant copper sculpture; its green color is oxidized copper, a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Cloud Gate: Anish Kapoor's stainless-steel 'Bean' in Chicago's Millennium Park; it is a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Balloon Dog: Jeff Koons's mirror-polished sculpture; an orange one sold for $58 million in 2013, a record for a living artist then.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Angel of the North: Antony Gormley's steel figure in Gateshead, about 20 meters tall; a sculpture, not a painting.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Christ the Redeemer: A soapstone-clad Rio statue, 30 meters tall, one of the New Seven Wonders; sculpture.
Famous paintings (not sculptures).Maman: Louise Bourgeois's giant steel spider; a sculpture, not a painting, that stands over nine meters tall.

Characters in The Hobbit.Bilbo Baggins: Bilbo Baggins stars here; the book begins with him as a comfort-loving homebody who is hired as a burglar by thirteen dwarves.
Characters in The Hobbit.Gandalf: Gandalf takes his name from a list of dwarf names in the Old Norse Völuspá, which Tolkien borrowed for many of the dwarves too.
Characters in The Hobbit.Thorin: Thorin Oakenshield leads the quest to reclaim Erebor, and dies after the Battle of Five Armies, having reconciled with Bilbo.
Characters in The Hobbit.Smaug: The dragon Smaug has a name Tolkien said was a joke: the past tense of the Germanic verb meaning to squeeze through a hole.
Characters in The Hobbit.Gollum: Gollum loses his ring to Bilbo in a riddle contest; Tolkien later rewrote this chapter so Gollum becomes obsessed instead of cheerfully offering it.
Characters in The Hobbit.Bard: Bard the Bowman kills Smaug with a black arrow after a thrush tells him about the dragon's missing scale.
Characters in The Hobbit.Beorn: Beorn is a skin-changer who is a huge man by day and a bear by night, and he helps the company in the Battle of Five Armies.
Characters in The Hobbit.Elrond: Elrond, lord of Rivendell, reads the moon-letters on Thorin's map and spots hidden runes that reveal the secret door into the Lonely Mountain.
Characters in The Hobbit.Balin: Balin, the dwarf who befriends Bilbo, later tries to resettle Moria and is killed there, as his tomb shows in The Fellowship of the Ring.
Characters in The Hobbit.Dwalin: Dwalin is among the dwarves who fight in the Battle of Five Armies and, unlike many of his companions, survives it.
Characters in The Hobbit.Fili: Fili and Kili are Thorin's sister's sons, and both fall in the final battle trying to shield their uncle.
Characters in The Hobbit.Kili: Kili is among the youngest of the thirteen dwarves, and he dies in the Battle of Five Armies guarding Thorin beside his brother Fili.
Characters in The Hobbit.Bombur: Bombur is the fattest dwarf, who falls into an enchanted stream in Mirkwood and sleeps for days, so the others must carry him.
Characters in The Hobbit.Frodo: Frodo is Bilbo's heir and hero of The Lord of the Rings, but he doesn't appear in The Hobbit, which only mentions him in passing.
Characters in The Hobbit.Sam: Samwise Gamgee is a Lord of the Rings character; Bilbo never meets him on his own adventure in The Hobbit.
Characters in The Hobbit.Aragorn: Aragorn belongs to The Lord of the Rings; in The Hobbit's time, he is a child, and he never appears.
Characters in The Hobbit.Boromir: Boromir is Denethor's son in The Lord of the Rings; his tale of the Fellowship's failure begins decades after Bilbo's quest.
Characters in The Hobbit.Éowyn: Éowyn, who kills the Witch-king, is a Rohan shieldmaiden of The Lord of the Rings, not The Hobbit.
Characters in The Hobbit.Faramir: Faramir is Boromir's brother in The Lord of the Rings, so he is absent from Bilbo's earlier adventure.
Characters in The Hobbit.Treebeard: Treebeard is an Ent of Fangorn in The Lord of the Rings; no Ents are encountered in The Hobbit.
Characters in The Hobbit.Gimli: Gimli's father Glóin joins Thorin's company, but Gimli himself belongs to The Lord of the Rings and not to Bilbo's story.
Characters in The Hobbit.Shelob: Shelob is the giant spider of Cirith Ungol in The Return of the King; The Hobbit has Mirkwood's spiders, not Shelob.
Characters in The Hobbit.Théoden: Théoden, king of Rohan, is a Lord of the Rings figure, and he and his horsemen never feature in The Hobbit.
Characters in The Hobbit.Merry: Merry, Frodo's cousin and a Fellowship member, is not in The Hobbit; he only appears in The Lord of the Rings.

Black and white things.Zebra: Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique, and the stripes may help deter biting flies, which seem to avoid landing on them.
Black and white things.Giant panda: Pandas eat bamboo for most of the day, up to about 12 kilograms of it, despite being classed as carnivores.
Black and white things.Penguin: The black back and white belly are camouflage, as predators below see white and ones above see dark.
Black and white things.Skunk: The skunk's black and white colouring is a warning, since it can spray a stinking liquid up to about three metres.
Black and white things.Dalmatian: Dalmatian puppies are born pure white and develop their spots as they grow, and they were once carriage escorts.
Black and white things.Piano keys: A standard piano has 88 keys, and 52 of them are white and 36 are black.
Black and white things.Orca: Orcas are the largest dolphins, and each pod has its own dialect, as they're not true whales.
Black and white things.Oreo: The cookie was first sold in 1912 and has become the best-selling cookie of the 20th century.
Black and white things.Domino: Dominoes carry white dots on black, or reversed, and the set of 28 tiles is the usual double-six.
Black and white things.Holstein cow: Holsteins, the black-and-white dairy cows, produce more milk than almost any other breed.
Black and white things.Magpie: Magpies are black and white with blue-green iridescence, and they are among the few birds that pass the mirror test.
Black and white things.Tuxedo: The tuxedo is named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where it was worn at a club in the 1880s.
Black and white things.Tiger: Tigers are orange with black stripes, and every tiger's stripe pattern is unique.
Black and white things.Red panda: The red panda is rusty red and not related to the giant panda, and it is closer to raccoons and weasels.
Black and white things.Polar bear: Polar bears look all white, but their skin is black, so no black pattern is visible.
Black and white things.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink, because of carotenoids in their diet.
Black and white things.Koala: Koalas are gray, and they sleep up to about 20 hours a day.
Black and white things.Ladybug: The usual ladybug is red with black spots, so it fails the white part.
Black and white things.Bumblebee: Bumblebees are black and yellow, and they can fly in cold weather by shivering.
Black and white things.Chipmunk: A chipmunk has brown fur with dark and light stripes, and cheek pouches to carry food.
Black and white things.Grizzly bear: Grizzlies are brown, and their name comes from their silver-tipped "grizzled" fur.
Black and white things.Toucan: Toucans have a black body and a huge colourful bill that helps them regulate body heat.
Black and white things.Goldfish: Goldfish are usually orange and gold, though they can be many colours.
Black and white things.Fox: Red foxes are rusty orange with a white tail tip, so they are not black and white.

Construction vehicles.Bulldozer: The name "bulldozer" is believed to come from "bulldose", a 1800s American term for a huge dose of something forceful.
Construction vehicles.Excavator: Excavators have a rotating cab, so the operator can dig a trench and swing the load without moving the tracks.
Construction vehicles.Crane: Tower cranes build themselves up, adding new mast sections as the building rises beneath them.
Construction vehicles.Dump truck: Some giant mining dump trucks have tyres taller than a house, and can carry loads of around 400 tonnes.
Construction vehicles.Cement mixer: A concrete truck's drum turns constantly to keep concrete from setting before it arrives.
Construction vehicles.Backhoe: A backhoe has a loader at the front and a digging arm at the back; it's the machine many Brits call a JCB.
Construction vehicles.Steamroller: Steamrollers used to be actual steam engines, but today the term covers any road roller that flattens asphalt.
Construction vehicles.Forklift: A forklift steers by its back wheels, which lets it turn within its own length, unlike a car.
Construction vehicles.Digger: "Digger" is the British word for a backhoe or excavator, and JCB's name comes from Joseph Cyril Bamford.
Construction vehicles.Grader: A grader's long blade, set between its axles, levels the ground to a precise slope for roads.
Construction vehicles.Cherry picker: The cherry picker is named after the machines that were once used to harvest cherries from tall trees in orchards.
Construction vehicles.Hearse: A hearse carries a coffin, and it isn't used on building sites; the word comes from a Latin term for a harrow.
Construction vehicles.Limousine: Limousine is named after the French region of Limousin; it's a luxury car, not a worksite machine.
Construction vehicles.Ambulance: An ambulance is an emergency medical vehicle; the word comes from the Latin "to walk".
Construction vehicles.Ice cream van: Ice cream vans play chimes to attract buyers, and there's no digging involved.
Construction vehicles.Taxi: "Taxi" comes from the taximeter, a device that measured distance; the vehicle moves people, not earth.
Construction vehicles.Tuk-tuk: The tuk-tuk is named after the sound of its engine, and it ferries tourists around Asian cities.
Construction vehicles.Rickshaw: The word rickshaw comes from Japanese "jinrikisha", meaning human-powered vehicle; it is a passenger carrier.
Construction vehicles.Golf cart: A golf cart carries golfers; many builders use them to get across big sites, but they don't count as construction vehicles.
Construction vehicles.Sports car: A sports car is built for speed, not heavy lifting, and certainly won't move a mound of earth.
Construction vehicles.Convertible: A convertible is a car with a folding roof; it carries passengers, not building materials.
Construction vehicles.Monorail: A monorail runs on a single rail, and the Wuppertal Schwebebahn in Germany has hung from it since 1901.
Construction vehicles.Double-decker: A double-decker is a two-storey bus, and London's red Routemaster is the best known; it carries passengers.
Construction vehicles.Gondola: A gondola is a Venetian rowing boat, or a cable-car cabin; it's no construction vehicle.

Architectural features.Column: Greek columns come in three orders, Doric, Ionic and Corinthian, distinguished by their capitals.
Architectural features.Arch: Romans perfected the arch because it turns weight into compression, letting stone span wide gaps without beams.
Architectural features.Dome: The Pantheon's concrete dome in Rome, nearly 2,000 years old, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
Architectural features.Spire: Salisbury Cathedral's spire is the tallest medieval church spire in England, at about 123 meters.
Architectural features.Gable: A gable is the triangular wall under a pitched roof, and the Dutch canal houses are famed for decorative ones.
Architectural features.Cornice: The cornice is the projecting molding at the top of a wall, and it also sheds rainwater away from the facade.
Architectural features.Buttress: Gothic builders added flying buttresses so walls could hold less stone and more window glass.
Architectural features.Vault: A vault is an arched ceiling in stone or brick, and the same word names a bank's safe, from Latin for 'turned'.
Architectural features.Lintel: A lintel is the beam over a door or window, and Stonehenge's horizontal stones are lintels, too.
Architectural features.Balcony: The word balcony comes from Italian, and a Juliet balcony, a tiny rail without a platform, is named for Shakespeare's heroine.
Architectural features.Atrium: Roman houses had an atrium, an open central hall, and malls and offices still borrow the idea.
Architectural features.Gargoyle: A gargoyle is a carved spout that throws rainwater away from walls; the word shares a root with 'gargle'.
Architectural features.Facade: The facade is a building's face, from the French for 'face', and some Hollywood sets have only a front.
Architectural features.Aileron: Ailerons are the flaps on aircraft wings that make the plane roll, a part of aviation, not architecture.
Architectural features.Fuselage: The fuselage is an aircraft's main body, and the word comes from the French for 'spindle-shaped'.
Architectural features.Rudder: A rudder steers a ship or aircraft by deflecting water or air, which is why it isn't a building part.
Architectural features.Keel: The keel is a ship's backbone, the beam along the bottom of a hull, so it's nautical rather than architectural.
Architectural features.Pantograph: A pantograph collects current from overhead lines for trams and trains, and also copies drawings.
Architectural features.Hubcap: A hubcap covers the center of a car wheel, so it belongs on vehicles, not buildings.
Architectural features.Spoke: Spokes link a wheel's hub to its rim; a bicycle wheel typically has 32 or 36 of them, none in a building.
Architectural features.Derailleur: A derailleur shifts a bicycle chain between gears, and the name is French for 'to derail'.
Architectural features.Crankshaft: The crankshaft turns an engine's up-and-down piston motion into spinning, so it belongs under a hood.
Architectural features.Bilge: The bilge is the lowest part of a ship's hull, where dirty water collects, and the word also means nonsense.
Architectural features.Mainsail: The mainsail is the biggest sail on a boat, so it's nautical and not architectural.

Types of earring.Stud: The simplest earring, just a small decoration that sits on the lobe with a post.
Types of earring.Hoop: Hoops are among the oldest earring shapes, with circles of metal in ancient Sumerian graves.
Types of earring.Drop: These dangle below the lobe, and the length can range from small to shoulder-grazing.
Types of earring.Chandelier: Named after the glittering light fixture, it is a cluster of gems that swings.
Types of earring.Huggie: Short for hugging, these small hoops cling close to the lobe.
Types of earring.Dangle: This style hangs freely and moves with you, which is why it is popular for parties.
Types of earring.Clip-on: These need no piercing; clip-ons were especially popular when piercing was out of fashion.
Types of earring.Threader: A threader is a fine chain you pull through the piercing, so it hangs down on both sides.
Types of earring.Ear cuff: An ear cuff wraps around the outer ear, so no piercing is needed.
Types of earring.Bangle: Bangles are stiff bracelets, and the name comes from the Hindi word bangri.
Types of earring.Choker: A choker sits tight around the neck and had its heyday in Victorian times and again in the 1990s.
Types of earring.Locket: A locket opens to hold a tiny photo or lock of hair, and it hangs from a chain.
Types of earring.Brooch: A brooch pins to clothing, and ancient Romans used brooches called fibulae to fasten cloaks.
Types of earring.Signet ring: A signet ring has an engraved crest, and was once pressed into hot wax to seal letters.
Types of earring.Tennis bracelet: This one is named for Chris Evert, who lost her diamond bracelet at the 1978 US Open and paused play.
Types of earring.Charm bracelet: Charms are added over the years, and they have been a keepsake tradition since Victorian times.
Types of earring.Anklet: An anklet circles the ankle, and anklets are old in India and Egypt.
Types of earring.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled half crown worn on the head, and not on ears.
Types of earring.Cameo: A cameo is a carved portrait in relief, and is generally pinned or hung, not worn on ears.
Types of earring.Toe ring: A toe ring is worn on the foot; in India it traditionally signals a married woman.
Types of earring.Lapel pin: A lapel pin attaches to a jacket collar, and not to the ear.
Types of earring.Cufflink: Cufflinks fasten the cuffs of a shirt and replaced buttons in the 17th century.
Types of earring.Tie clip: A tie clip holds a tie against a shirt, and is a menswear accessory.
Types of earring.Pocket watch: The pocket watch fell from favor once wristwatches took over around the 1910s.

Types of boot.Wellington: Named for the Duke of Wellington, who asked his cobbler to trim a Hessian boot; the waterproof rubber version came later.
Types of boot.Chelsea: The elastic-sided Chelsea boot was reportedly designed for Queen Victoria in the 1850s and later became a 1960s mod and Beatles favorite.
Types of boot.Cowboy: Cowboy boots have a tall shaft and angled heel so the foot slides easily into stirrups and stays there.
Types of boot.Ugg: Ugg boots are sheepskin boots that surfers in Australia popularized for warming feet after a swim.
Types of boot.Combat: Combat boots became fashion after soldiers wore them; Dr. Martens began as a comfort boot with an air-cushioned sole in 1960.
Types of boot.Hiking: A good hiking boot has stiff soles and ankle support; breaking them in before a long trek helps avoid blisters.
Types of boot.Ski: Ski boots clip the foot rigidly to the ski, and the plastic shell is much stiffer than any other footwear.
Types of boot.Riding: Riding boots are tall so the leg grips the saddle without pinching; the heel stops the foot slipping through the stirrup.
Types of boot.Desert: Desert boots are soft suede ankle boots, made popular by Clarks in 1950 after British officers in Cairo wore a similar style.
Types of boot.Chukka: Chukka boots are ankle-high with two or three eyelet pairs, said to be named for chukkers, the periods in polo.
Types of boot.Go-go: Go-go boots are white, mid-calf and glossy, made famous by Courrèges in the 1960s, and tied to the go-go dancing craze.
Types of boot.Thigh-high: Thigh-high boots began as riding gear for men in the 1600s, and later became a 1960s fashion icon.
Types of boot.Snow: Snow boots are insulated and waterproof, often with a thick lug sole to grip ice.
Types of boot.Loafer: A loafer is a slip-on shoe with no laces, not a boot; it came from Norwegian fishermen's slippers.
Types of boot.Pump: A pump is a low-cut shoe, so it isn't a boot; the name may come from pumping action or a French word.
Types of boot.Mule: A mule is a backless shoe, so it can't be a boot; the name is from the stubborn animal's heels.
Types of boot.Ballet flat: Ballet flats, based on dancers' slippers, are low shoes that Audrey Hepburn made fashion in the 1950s.
Types of boot.Espadrille: Espadrilles have rope soles and canvas uppers, from the Pyrenees; their name comes from the esparto grass used.
Types of boot.Slingback: A slingback is a shoe with a strap around the heel instead of a closed back, so it can't be a boot.
Types of boot.Flip-flop: Flip-flops are similar to ancient Egyptian sandals; their name comes from the sound they make on the foot.
Types of boot.Oxford: Oxfords are lace-up shoes named after Oxford University, where students in the 1800s favored them over boots.
Types of boot.Derby: A Derby has open lacing, which differs from an Oxford's closed lacing; it is a shoe, not a boot.
Types of boot.Mary Jane: Mary Janes are strap shoes named for a comic-strip character from 1902 and so aren't boots.
Types of boot.Sandal: Sandals are among the oldest footwear: preserved examples in Oregon are about 10,000 years old.

Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Chipmunk: The Eastern chipmunk stuffs its cheek pouches with seeds, which can stretch to hold several times the size of its head.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Marmot: This large ground squirrel hibernates for around eight months in alpine burrows, and whistles alarms to its colony.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Prairie dog: Actually a ground squirrel, whose colony calls include specific words for predators, such as a tall human in a blue shirt.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Groundhog: Another name is woodchuck, and it's the animal that Punxsutawney Phil represents each February 2.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Red squirrel: Eurasian red squirrels have tufted ears, and in Britain have been displaced by the introduced grey squirrel.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Flying squirrel: It doesn't fly but glides on a skin flap between its limbs for dozens of metres from tree to tree.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Fox squirrel: North America's largest tree squirrel, with a big bushy tail and sometimes a black coat.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Gray squirrel: Many tree seeds are planted by forgetful gray squirrels, which bury thousands of nuts each autumn.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Ground squirrel: Thirteen-lined ground squirrels hibernate with body temperatures near freezing, and their heart rate drops to a handful of beats a minute.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Woodchuck: The old saying asks how much wood it could chuck, but the name actually comes from an Algonquian word for the animal.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Beaver: Though a rodent, it belongs to a different family; it builds dams and lodges, and its teeth never stop growing.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Porcupine: A rodent in the Old World or New World families, with quills, and not related to squirrels closely.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Hamster: Belongs to the family Cricetidae, along with voles, and has pouches like chipmunks, but not Sciuridae.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Guinea pig: A rodent from the Andes, in the cavy family and not related to pigs or squirrels.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Capybara: The world's largest rodent, weighing up to about 65 kilograms, is a cavy relative not a squirrel.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Gerbil: A desert rodent in the mouse-like family and not in the squirrel family.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Mouse: Mice are in the family Muridae and not squirrels, and are the most numerous mammals in many places.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Rat: Rats are Muridae, the same family as mice and not squirrels.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Chinchilla: An Andean rodent whose fur is among the densest of any land animal, with up to 60 hairs per follicle, but not a squirrel.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Lemming: Famous for the myth of mass suicide, which is false; it is a vole relative, not a squirrel.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Muskrat: A semi-aquatic rodent of the vole family, not a squirrel or a true rat.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Mole: Not a rodent at all; moles belong to a group of insect-eaters, and not squirrels.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Rabbit: Rabbits and hares are not rodents, but lagomorphs, with a second pair of tiny upper incisors.
Squirrel family members (Sciuridae).Hare: Hares are lagomorphs rather than rodents, and can run up to roughly 70 kilometres per hour.

The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Arthur Dent: The hapless Englishman whose house is demolished on the same day as Earth; Martin Freeman played him in the 2005 film.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Ford Prefect: An alien researcher who picked his name from a Ford car, thinking cars were Earth's dominant life form.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Zaphod Beeblebrox: The two-headed, three-armed ex-President of the Galaxy who stole the Heart of Gold.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Marvin: The depressed robot with 'a brain the size of a planet'; Alan Rickman voiced him in the 2005 film.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Trillian: Tricia McMillan, a human astrophysicist who left Earth with Zaphod before its destruction.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Babel fish: A small yellow fish placed in the ear that translates any language; the book jokes that its existence disproves God.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Vogons: Bureaucratic aliens who destroy Earth for a hyperspace bypass; their poetry is the third worst in the universe.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Heart of Gold: A stolen starship powered by the Infinite Improbability Drive.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Magrathea: A legendary planet where bespoke planets are built, including a replacement Earth.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Slartibartfast: The Magrathean planet designer who won an award for Norway's fjords.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Deep Thought: The supercomputer that calculates the answer to life, the universe and everything: 42.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Improbability Drive: A propulsion system that makes the improbable happen, like turning missiles into a whale and a bowl of petunias.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Towel: The most useful thing a hitchhiker can own; fans celebrate Towel Day every May 25 in Adams's honor.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Han Solo: Star Wars smuggler; Harrison Ford worked as a carpenter before landing the role.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Chewbacca: The Wookiee's voice was built by Ben Burtt from blended animal recordings, including bears.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Spock: Star Trek's half-Vulcan science officer; Leonard Nimoy invented the Vulcan nerve pinch.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Captain Kirk: Captain of the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, played by William Shatner from 1966; a different franchise.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Dalek: Doctor Who's metal-cased villains were created in 1963; Douglas Adams was a Doctor Who script editor, making this a tempting mix-up.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.R2-D2: A Star Wars droid; the Guide's famous robot is Marvin.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.HAL 9000: The computer of 2001: A Space Odyssey; fans note its name is one letter off each of IBM's, which Clarke denied was deliberate.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Paul Atreides: The hero of Frank Herbert's Dune, from 1965, not the Guide.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Rick Sanchez: A mad scientist from Rick and Morty; the show has cosmic absurdity like the Guide, but is separate.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Ender Wiggin: Orson Scott Card's child commander, from Ender's Game, a different sci-fi universe.
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.Bender: Futurama's drinking robot, a cynical machine like Marvin, but from a different universe.

Days of Holy Week.Palm Sunday: It starts Holy Week and marks Jesus entering Jerusalem as crowds waved palm branches.
Days of Holy Week.Holy Monday: Traditionally recalls Jesus cursing a fig tree and driving the money changers out of the Temple.
Days of Holy Week.Holy Tuesday: The day Christians remember Jesus teaching in the Temple and giving the parables of the end times.
Days of Holy Week.Spy Wednesday: Named for Judas, who agreed that day to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
Days of Holy Week.Maundy Thursday: Maundy comes from the Latin mandatum, meaning command, from Jesus telling his disciples to love one another at the Last Supper.
Days of Holy Week.Good Friday: The day of the crucifixion. 'Good' here probably means holy, though nobody is fully sure.
Days of Holy Week.Holy Saturday: The quiet day between the crucifixion and Easter, when Jesus is remembered lying in the tomb.
Days of Holy Week.Holy Thursday: It is another name for Maundy Thursday, the day of the Last Supper, and so it counts as part of Holy Week.
Days of Holy Week.Holy Wednesday: This is an alternative name for Spy Wednesday, so it belongs in Holy Week too.
Days of Holy Week.Ash Wednesday: It begins Lent, 46 days before Easter, so it falls well before Holy Week, with ashes marked on foreheads.
Days of Holy Week.Shrove Tuesday: It is the day before Lent begins, when people used up rich foods, which is why pancakes are traditional.
Days of Holy Week.Epiphany: It falls on 6 January, marking the visit of the Magi, so it comes weeks after Christmas, not in Holy Week.
Days of Holy Week.Pentecost: It comes seven weeks after Easter and remembers the Holy Spirit descending on the apostles.
Days of Holy Week.Advent Sunday: The first Sunday of Advent starts the Christian year in late November or early December, long before Easter.
Days of Holy Week.Christmas Eve: It sits on 24 December, so it belongs to the Christmas season and not to the spring days of Holy Week.
Days of Holy Week.Boxing Day: It falls on 26 December. The name probably comes from boxes of gifts or money given to servants and the poor.
Days of Holy Week.All Saints Day: On 1 November it honours all saints, and it gave us Halloween, short for All Hallows' Eve.
Days of Holy Week.Candlemas: On 2 February it marks Jesus's presentation at the Temple, and weather lore connected to it inspired Groundhog Day.
Days of Holy Week.Easter Monday: It follows Easter Sunday so it comes right after Holy Week, and it is a public holiday in many countries.
Days of Holy Week.Ascension Day: It falls 40 days after Easter, a Thursday, and it marks Jesus rising to heaven.
Days of Holy Week.Trinity Sunday: It comes a week after Pentecost, so about two months after Holy Week, and it celebrates the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one.
Days of Holy Week.Corpus Christi: Its name is Latin for body of Christ, and it comes in late spring, about 60 days after Easter.
Days of Holy Week.Laetare Sunday: The fourth Sunday of Lent, called Rose Sunday, when priests could wear rose-pink vestments. It is weeks before Holy Week.
Days of Holy Week.Fat Tuesday: Mardi Gras is the English translation. It is the last feast before Lent, so it comes about six weeks ahead of Holy Week.
